sweeps.topic: Starlink latency/jitter/packet loss for mobile terminals and voice traffic (2025-2026), and hosted Realtime-voice session lifetime / reconnect / re-priming / caching design (OpenAI Realtime, Gemini Live)

findings.claim: Starlink end-to-end latency follows a deterministic 15-second period: the first 140 ms and last 75 ms of each period are spike regions averaging +74 ms above mean latency, and a period-aware predictor reaches p99 prediction error < 50 ms.
findings.source_title: Statistical Characterization and Prediction of E2E Latency over LEO Satellite Networks (Casparsen, Jakobsen, Nielsen, Popovski, Leyva Mayorga; Aalborg; npj Wireless Technology 2026)
findings.numbers: 500 Hz one-way probes (2 ms spacing), NTP sub-ms sync; boundary regions = first 140 ms + last 75 ms of each 15 s period (derived 215 ms = 1.4 % of time); spike avg 74 ms above mean; p99 prediction error < 50 ms; MSE ~65 ms^2 after 1 s, ~21 ms^2 after 5 s (~8 / ~4.5 ms); GMM(3) classifies period to AUPRC 0.95 in 1.6 s
findings.relevance: Defines the jitter envelope Model B's voice jitter buffer must absorb and gives Model A a way to phase cloud plan-lane calls away from spike windows.

findings.claim: Voice/video over Starlink breaks on link gaps longer than ~1 s, while gaps shorter than 0.5 s are absorbed; audio loss rate tracks Starlink outages directly; 2022-23 app-reported outages averaged 6.46 s (max 18 s), and RTT steps ~30 ms every ~15 s with occasional 180 ms jumps.
findings.source_title: Realtime Multimedia Services over Starlink: A Reality Check (Zhao, Fang, Wang, Liu; ACM NOSSDAV 2023)
findings.numbers: 4-month campaign from Dec 2022, two dishes (urban Pacific West Coast, rural US Mid-South), 887,628 ping samples; outages avg 6.46 s, longest 18 s; Zoom 'significant variations ... outages lasting longer than 1 second', '<0.5 seconds have marginal impacts'; interactive RTT 0.69 s vs 0.57 s terrestrial (var 0.0095 vs 0.0073); terrestrial made 23.5 % more interactions; RTT steady-state steps ~30 ms every ~15 s, spikes to 180 ms
findings.relevance: Sets the >1 s gap threshold at which Model B must fail over to the local cascade voice and mute/truncate the hosted session.

findings.claim: A moving Starlink terminal spent ~2.7 % of a 5-hour drive in outage, with SKY_SEARCH (transient obstruction) at 45.18 % of outage time (doubled vs stationary); hard-obstruction beam switches fall to a backup beam with markedly lower performance and recovery is often delayed until the next scheduled handover.
findings.source_title: Demystifying Starlink Network Performance under Vehicular Mobility with Dynamic Beam Switching (Zhao et al.)
findings.numbers: ~500 km / 5 h, midwestern USA (rural/urban/suburban/highway); mobile UT outages: SKY_SEARCH 221.4 s (45.18 %), NO_DOWNLINK 134.0 s (27.33 %), OBSTRUCTED 110.9 s (22.62 %), NO_PINGS 23.7 s (4.83 %) -> derived ~490 s / 18,000 s = 2.7 %; stationary obstructed UT (17.9 % FOV): OBSTRUCTED 367.8 s (56.21 %), SKY_SEARCH 148.2 s, NO_DOWNLINK 132.3 s, NO_PINGS 6.0 s
findings.relevance: Quantifies how often the hosted voice will simply be absent on an outdoor walk; forces the local-fallback contract for Model B and no cloud dependency in Model A.

findings.claim: Motion itself costs little on Starlink (median RTT +9 ms, throughput -9/-3.2 Mbps in motion; ~10 % throughput drop with no further speed dependence); obstruction is the loss driver (~1 % rural clear sky, up to 10 % urban, ~45 % near mountains with RTT to 349 ms).
findings.source_title: Starlink in Northern Europe: A New Look at Stationary and In-motion Performance (Ullah et al., VTT / Univ. Oulu); corroborated by Starlink on the Road (Laniewski et al., arXiv 2403.13497)
findings.numbers: FHP terminal, 24 May-27 Jun 2024; stationary median RTT Oulu 90 / Helsinki 85 / Frankfurt 55 / Amsterdam 60 / Reykjavik 99 / New York 143 ms; in motion +9 ms RTT, -9 Mbps DL, -3.2 Mbps UL; Osnabrueck (https://arxiv.org/html/2403.13497v1): 15,269 samples (27 % in motion), DL 265-270 vs 299 Mbit/s, UL 15.40 vs 17.74; speed corr -0.15/-0.12; loss ~1 % rural, <=10 % urban, ~45 % mountains, RTT to 349 ms; dish power 113 W avg, in-motion median 137 W
findings.relevance: A walking dog is a slow mobile terminal; the design driver is line-of-sight (trees, buildings), not speed.

findings.claim: In controlled Zoom tests Starlink uplink one-way delay was 52 +/- 14 ms vs 27 +/- 7 ms terrestrial with ~27 FPS on both, OWD shifts at globally synchronised 15 s reconfiguration boundaries, cloud-gaming RTT 50 +/- 16 ms with FPS drops < 20 at those boundaries, and reconfigurations cause brief sub-second disruptions.
findings.source_title: A Multifaceted Look at Starlink Performance (Mohan et al., ACM WWW 2024)
findings.numbers: 19.2 M M-Lab tests, 34 countries; Zoom UL OWD 52+/-14 vs 27+/-7 ms, DL 35+/-11 vs 32+/-7 ms, ~27 FPS, FEC 146+/-99 kbps vs 2+/-2 kbps; Luna: RTT 11/39/50 ms (terrestrial/5G/Starlink), freezes 0+/-0 / 0+/-220 / 0+/-120 ms/min, game delay 133.5/165.8/167.1 ms; bent-pipe 36-48 ms (median ~40); bufferbloat under load
findings.relevance: Closest published proxy for WebRTC voice over Starlink; shows FEC/jitter buffering already copes with baseline jitter and that the 15 s boundary is the residual problem.

findings.claim: Official Starlink 2024-2025 figures: US peak-hour median latency cut from 48.5 ms to 33 ms and p99 from >150 ms to <65 ms (2024), reaching 25.7 ms median peak-hour by June 2025; latency is measured from millions of routers every 15 s; buffers were right-sized to reduce bufferbloat.
findings.source_title: Improving Starlink's Latency (Starlink engineering note); 2025 figure via The Register quoting Starlink's network update (https://www.theregister.com/2025/07/16/starlink_network_update/)
findings.numbers: goal 20 ms median; US peak-hour median 48.5 -> 33 ms (>30 %), p99 >150 -> <65 ms (>60 %); outside US median -25 %, worst-case -35 %; propagation 1.8-3.6 ms per leg, <10 ms RTT; 6 new US PoPs 2024; fq_codel on WiFi router; Jul 2025: median peak-hour 25.7 ms, 200 Mbps median download, 6 M+ customers, 7,800+ satellites
findings.relevance: Baseline RTT budget for Model B: ~26-35 ms typical, <65 ms p99 in clear sky, before the 15 s spike.

findings.claim: In a 2025 Copenhagen campaign Starlink one-way delay medians were 36/43 ms (urban DL/UL) and 26/32 ms suburban, but 99/376 ms with 49 % coverage loss under forest; urban outage probability for a 5 Mbps flow was 12-17 %, and the authors judge cellular superior for real-time applications.
findings.source_title: Towards Reliable Connectivity: Measurement-Driven Assessment of Starlink and OneWeb Non-Terrestrial and 5G Terrestrial Networks (Ramirez-Arroyo et al.)
findings.numbers: 3-day campaign; urban Starlink DL 36 / UL 43 ms median, outage 12-17 %; suburban 26 / 32 ms, coverage loss 3 %; forest 99 / 376 ms, coverage loss 49 %; Starlink+OneWeb multi-connectivity cuts urban outage from 12-21 % to 2 %
findings.relevance: Worst-case environments (park with tree cover) for a companion dog; argues for cellular or dual-WAN as the voice uplink where available.

findings.claim: Long-run RIPE Atlas / Cloudflare Radar data (2022-mid 2024) show Starlink TLS-handshake latency of 26 ms min / 80 ms median / 100 ms mean with a bimodal 80-100 ms and 150-250 ms distribution, packet loss of 1-4 % in most countries (0.23 % Czechia to 18.27 % Philippines, >10 % Germany), and no statistically significant latency-loss correlation.
findings.source_title: Breaking Through the Clouds: Performance Insights into Starlink's Latency and Packet Loss (Richter, Ververis, Bajpai; IFIP Networking 2025)
findings.numbers: 146 RIPE Atlas probes in AS14593, 2022-01-01 to 2024-06-30; TLS latency 26 ms min, 80 ms median, 100 ms mean (2024); medians 81-84 ms (2022), 94-98 ms (2023); loss: Czechia 0.23 %, Chile 0.24 %, Sweden 0.53 %, Austria 0.73 %, Belgium 2.27 %, Australia 3.97 %, Netherlands 14.19 %, Philippines 18.27 %, Germany >10 %
findings.relevance: Independent long-baseline loss figures; packet loss of a few percent is the norm and must be covered by Opus FEC / PLC rather than assumed away.

findings.claim: OpenAI Realtime sessions are hard-capped at 60 minutes (30 on Azure), killed with an error event code session_expired; session.update does not extend the timer; the context window is 32,768 tokens with 28,672 max input and 16,384 for instructions+tools, and automatic truncation busts the prompt cache.
findings.source_title: OpenAI Realtime conversations guide; Developer notes on the Realtime API (https://developers.openai.com/blog/realtime-api); Azure Q&A (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/answers/questions/5741275/gpt-realtime-maximum-session-length-30-minutes); session_expired thread (https://community.openai.com/t/realtime-api-session-expired/975036)
findings.numbers: 'The maximum duration of a Realtime session is 60 minutes' (up from 30); Azure 'The maximum session duration is 30 minutes' (Q&A 26 Jan 2026); error {type:error, code:session_expired, message:'Your session hit the maximum duration of N minutes.'}; window 32,768, max response 4,096, max input 28,672, instructions+tools 16,384; auto-truncate at 28,672; retention_ratio 0.8; truncation 'disabled' option; voice cannot change after first audio
findings.relevance: Forces a proactive session-rotation design for Model B's all-day narration; nothing server-side carries context across the boundary.

findings.claim: Instruction re-priming on a fresh OpenAI Realtime session is nearly free if the instruction prefix is byte-identical and >= 1,024 tokens: the prefix (instructions + session preamble) is cached across sessions on the same backend host and billed at the cached rate ($0.40/1M audio or text vs $32/1M audio, $4/1M text) for ~30 min after last use; editing instructions mid-session reduces the cache rate.
findings.source_title: Microsoft Q&A: first-turn cached_input_tokens in a Realtime session (25 Mar 2026); OpenAI prompt caching guide (https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching); Realtime costs guide (https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/realtime-costs); pricing (https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/pricing)
findings.numbers: 'If the prefix exceeds the minimum caching threshold (1,024 tokens) and matches a prefix that was recently processed on the same backend host, then the model will report cached input tokens, even on the very first turn'; cache reads 0.1x; lifetime 30 min after last use (GPT-5.6+), 5-10 min up to 1 h earlier models; gpt-realtime-2.1/2: audio $32 in / $0.40 cached / $64 out, text $4 / $0.40 / $24; mini audio $10 / $0.30 / $20; user audio 1 token per 100 ms (600/min), assistant audio 1 token per 50 ms (1,200/min); whole conversation re-sent per Response; derived re-prime of a 3k-token preamble ~$0.012 uncached vs ~$0.0012 cached
findings.relevance: Makes 20-50 min rotation with a static instruction block and text summary the cheap, correct pattern; dynamic robot state must live in later items, not in instructions.

findings.claim: LiveKit's production fix for Realtime expiry rotates proactively on a timer (default 20 min, configurable), waits for the current generation to finish, replays chat history into the new session and emits session_reconnected, rather than reacting to the expiry error.
findings.source_title: livekit/agents PR #2360 (auto reconnect for OpenAI Realtime; fixes issue #2341)
findings.numbers: RealtimeModel(max_session_duration=20*60) default 20 min, None disables; merged 30 May 2025; error text at the time 'Your session hit the maximum duration of 30 minutes.'
findings.relevance: Reference pattern for Model B's session-cycling: rotate at a natural pause with history replay, never on the error.

findings.claim: OpenAI ephemeral client secrets default to 600 s (10 s to 7,200 s); a running session continues after the secret expires and one secret can open multiple sessions until it expires.
findings.source_title: OpenAI API reference: Create client secret
findings.numbers: expires_after.seconds default 600, range 10-7200; anchor 'created_at'; 'The session itself may continue after that time once started. A secret can be used to create multiple sessions until it expires.'; truncation 'auto'|'disabled'; RetentionRatioTruncation.retention_ratio 0.0-1.0
findings.relevance: The Orin-side gateway can mint one secret per rotation window and pre-open the replacement session without a new round trip.

findings.claim: Gemini Live's binding limit is the ~10-minute WebSocket connection (GoAway with timeLeft ~60 s before ABORTED), not the ~15-min audio-only / ~2-min audio+video figures, which are just the 128k context filling at ~25 audio tokens/s; sessions become unlimited with context-window compression (default trigger 80 % of window, target = trigger/2) and resume via a handle valid 2 h (24 h on Agent Platform).
findings.source_title: Gemini Live API session management; Live API reference (https://ai.google.dev/api/live); Firebase limits (https://firebase.google.com/docs/ai-logic/live-api/limits-and-specs); Firebase sessions (https://firebase.google.com/docs/ai-logic/live-api/sessions); best practices (https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/live-api/best-practices); Google staff forum reply (https://discuss.ai.google.dev/t/gemini-live-api-sessions-exceeding-15-minute-limit-without-compression/114104)
findings.numbers: 'audio-only sessions are limited to 15 minutes', 'audio-video sessions are limited to 2 minutes'; 'lifetime of a connection is limited ... to around 10 minutes'; going-away notice 'about 60 seconds before'; 'Resumption tokens are valid for 2 hr' (Developer API), 24 h Agent Platform, ~10 min after a drop; triggerTokens default 80 % of context, targetTokens default trigger/2; example trigger 25,000 / window 8,000; 128k context native audio, 32k others; ~25 audio tokens/s; 1,000 concurrent sessions and 4M TPM per Firebase project; send audio in 20-40 ms chunks; Google staff: '15 min is an approximation. It really depends on the context window size'
findings.relevance: Gemini is the only hosted voice with server-side resumption; a Model B on Gemini must always run compression and reconnect on GoAway with the last handle.

findings.claim: Gemini Live re-bills the entire cumulative context (retained raw audio tokens plus system instruction) at the standard audio input rate on every turn, so cost scales with turn count rather than call duration and there is no cached-prefix discount; audio input is $3.00/1M ($0.005/min) and audio output $12.00/1M ($0.018/min) on gemini-3.1-flash-live-preview.
findings.source_title: Google AI Developers Forum: Gemini Live native-audio billing (Google staff reply, 7 Jul 2026); Gemini pricing (https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/pricing); caching doc (https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/caching)
findings.numbers: 'Gemini Live re-bills the entire cumulative context on every single turn'; 5.8-min call cost 37 % less than a 5.6-min call; 3.1-flash-live: text in $0.75, audio in $3.00 ($0.005/min), video $1.00 ($0.002/min), text out $4.50, audio out $12.00 ($0.018/min); 2.5-flash-native-audio: text $0.50 / audio $3.00 in, text $2.00 / audio $12.00 out; implicit caching min 2,048 (2.5) / 4,096 (3.x) tokens with no Live-API statement
findings.relevance: On Gemini the compressed-window size is a cost knob: keep it small and prefer a text summary over raw audio history when rotating.

design_implications: Model A's 10 Hz act loop must never touch Starlink: even clear-sky links carry a deterministic +74 ms spike for ~215 ms every 15 s plus sub-second reconfiguration disruptions, and a moving terminal is in outage ~2.7 % of the time; the 0.5-2 Hz plan lane may consult a hosted model only as an optional hint with a local default, treating any gap > 1 s as 'cloud absent' for that tick.

Phase cloud calls to the 15 s Starlink cycle: the period is globally synchronised and classifiable in ~1.6 s with p99 error < 50 ms, so schedule plan-lane requests and receipt-narration bursts to complete outside the first 140 ms / last 75 ms of each period.

Model B transport: WebRTC (UDP) not WebSocket; a 100-150 ms adaptive jitter buffer covers the +74 ms boundary spike and ~30 ms RTT steps on a 26-50 ms baseline; local VAD/barge-in on the XVF3800 stays authoritative because hosted models cannot see link gaps; on a hole > 1 s, mute uplink, truncate the unplayed response on reconnect, and let the local cascade voice carry the narration.

The robot must shape its own uplink: Starlink queues are drop-front with no per-flow fair queuing and bufferbloat under load, so rate-limit telemetry/log egress and keep voice packets out of the boundary windows.

OpenAI session rotation: rotate proactively at a natural pause well before the 60-min cap (30 on Azure; LiveKit uses a 20-min timer), replay a text summary + last N turns as conversation items, keep the instruction block byte-identical and >= 1,024 tokens so the new session hits the ~30-min prompt cache (re-prime cost ~$0.001 vs ~$0.012 for a 3k-token preamble), and put per-minute robot state in later items rather than in instructions; mint client secrets (default 600 s, up to 7,200 s) on the Orin gateway so one secret can open the replacement session.

Gemini session design: the binding limit is the ~10-min connection with a ~60 s GoAway warning; always enable context-window compression (e.g. trigger 25k / target 8k) and reconnect with the latest resumption handle (valid 2 h); because every turn re-bills the full retained audio context at standard rate, keep the compressed window small and prefer text summaries over audio history.

Cost and fallback contract: the local VAD gate (stream only when the owner addresses the dog) is the biggest cost lever for both vendors (Gemini listens at $0.005/min, OpenAI first-pass $0.0192/min with 80x cheaper cached re-reads); given 2.7 % outage in motion, 12-17 % urban one-way outage at 5 Mbps and 49 % forest coverage loss, Model B's narration contract must be satisfiable by the on-Orin cascade, with the hosted voice as quality-on-top.

Open measurements to run locally: no source measured WebRTC/Opus over Starlink at walking speed or with a low-mounted (dog-height) dish, the OpenAI WebRTC reconnect gap (ICE + session.created + first cached response) is unpublished, and whether Gemini resumption handles survive a Starlink CGNAT IP change after an outage is undocumented; a one-hour 100 Hz OWD log over the owner's terminal aligned to 15 s boundaries would close the first two.

results.claim: Starlink end-to-end latency follows a deterministic 15-second period: the first 140 ms and last 75 ms of each period are spike regions averaging +74 ms above mean latency, and a period-aware predictor reaches p99 prediction error < 50 ms.
results.evidence_quote: "introduce a segmentation of the deterministic 15-second periodic behavior observed in Starlink. We characterize handover-induced boundary regions that produce latency spikes lasting approximately 140 ms at the beginning and 75 ms at the end of each cycle" ... "exhibit a sharp peak at the start of each interval, reaching an average of 74 ms above the mean latency, followed by a rapid decline and a secondary rise near the end of the period." ... "The red regions in Fig. 3 correspond to the first 140 ms and the last 75 ms of each period; these edge windows are excluded from subsequent analysis to focus on the stable intra-period regime." ... "by exploiting the periodic structure, isolating boundary regions, and applying lightweight parametric and non-parametric models to intra-period latency distributions, we achieve 99th-percentile latency prediction errors below 50 ms." (arxiv.org/html/2601.08439; also verified: "Probe packets were transmitted at 2 ms intervals, corresponding to a sampling rate of 500 Hz"; "MSE of ≈65 ms² after 1 s and ≈21 ms² after 5 s"; "GMM ... with 3 kernels is the fastest to achieve an AUPRC of 0.95, taking just 1.6 s")
results.correction: Two details are off. (1) The +74 ms average applies only to the sharp peak at the START of each period; the end-of-period region (last 75 ms) is described only as a 'secondary rise' with no separate magnitude given. (2) The p99 < 50 ms prediction error is achieved for the stable INTRA-period regime after the boundary windows (first 140 ms + last 75 ms) are excluded from analysis; it is not a bound that covers the spike windows themselves. Corrected statement: 'Starlink latency shows a deterministic 15 s period; the first 140 ms and last 75 ms of each period are handover-induced spike windows (the start-of-period peak averages +74 ms above mean); excluding those windows, lightweight intra-period models reach p99 prediction error < 50 ms.' The derived '215 ms = 1.4 %' figure is arithmetic, not stated in the paper.

results.claim: Voice/video over Starlink breaks on link gaps longer than ~1 s, while gaps shorter than 0.5 s are absorbed; audio loss rate tracks Starlink outages directly; 2022-23 app-reported outages averaged 6.46 s (max 18 s), and RTT steps ~30 ms every ~15 s with occasional 180 ms jumps.
results.evidence_quote: "Our measurement started from December 2022 and lasted 4 months." ... "Dish A in an urban area of Pacific West Coast, whereas Dish B in a rural area of the US Mid-South." ... "the red dots indicate the network outages reported from the Starlink mobile application ... For Starlink Ethernet, we observed the average of the outage time is about 6.46 seconds, with the longest outage being 18s." ... "Starlink network exhibits significant variations, particularly during network outages lasting longer than 1 second. However, Starlink network outages shorter than 0.5 seconds have marginal impacts on the Zoom meeting performance. Furthermore, we can see that unlike screen share latency, the audio loss rate is highly correlated with Starlink network outages." ... Table 3: Average of RTT (s) 0.57 (terrestrial) vs 0.69 (Starlink Ethernet); Variance 0.0073 vs 0.0095; "The terrestrial network made about 23.5% more interactions than the Starlink network" ... "the primary link will shift to next nearest satellite for roughly every 15 seconds. In addition, the RTT difference between each steady state in Figure 8 is approximately 30ms" ... "in sample A, the RTT increases to 180ms at 01:00 and leads to a 5-second buffer drop." ... "eventually collected 887,628 data points" (PDF text extracted with pdftotext; NOSSDAV '23, Zhao, Fang, Wang, Liu; doi 10.1145/3592473.3592562)
results.correction: All numbers check out. Two wording nuances: the paper says Zoom shows 'significant variations' (video pauses / audio cut-offs) on outages > 1 s rather than that voice 'breaks'; and '180 ms' is the absolute RTT level reached in the Twitch example ('RTT increases to 180ms'), not a 180 ms delta — phrase it as 'occasional jumps to ~180 ms'. The 6.46 s / 18 s outage statistics are from the Starlink-app-reported outages on Dish A (Starlink Ethernet) during the VoD experiments.

results.claim: A moving Starlink terminal spent ~2.7 % of a 5-hour drive in outage, with SKY_SEARCH (transient obstruction) at 45.18 % of outage time (doubled vs stationary); hard-obstruction beam switches fall to a backup beam with markedly lower performance and recovery is often delayed until the next scheduled handover.
results.evidence_quote: "approximately 500 km of driving over 5 hours across rural, urban, suburban, and highway environments in the midwestern USA" ... "Table 1 summarizes the outage event statistics observed in both mobile and stationary obstructed scenarios. Both statistics are collected over a 5-hour measurement period." Table 1 (mobile UT): SKY_SEARCH 221.404 s (45.175%), NO_DOWNLINK 133.958 s (27.333%), OBSTRUCTED 110.858 s (22.620%), NO_PINGS 23.659 s (4.827%); stationary obstructed UT (17.9% FOV): OBSTRUCTED 367.764 s (56.212%), SKY_SEARCH 148.222 s (22.655%), NO_DOWNLINK 132.265 s (20.216%), NO_PINGS 5.999 s (0.917%). ... "This can result in a doubling of SKY_SEARCH events, accounting for up to 45.18% of the total outage time, compared to a stationary UT that is heavily obstructed by trees with a 17.9% FOV obstruction ratio" ... "This suggests that the UT, when forced to conduct a beam switch due to a hard obstruction event, falls back to a non-primary or backup beam in the serving cell with markedly lower performance." ... "Following this switch, the downlink throughput drops to roughly half of that observed with STARLINK-35320." ... "Throughput recovery is frequently delayed until the next scheduled handover, when bicasting and coordinated ground-station selection again become available."
results.correction: No correction needed. Note only that the '~2.7 %' is derived (489.9 s summed outage / 18,000 s = 2.72 %), not stated by the paper; and 'doubled vs stationary' refers to the paper's comparison against a heavily tree-obstructed stationary UT (SKY_SEARCH share 45.18 % vs 22.66 %), not an unobstructed one.

results.claim: OpenAI Realtime sessions are hard-capped at 60 minutes (30 on Azure), killed with an error event code session_expired; session.update does not extend the timer; the context window is 32,768 tokens with 28,672 max input and 16,384 for instructions+tools, and automatic truncation busts the prompt cache.
results.evidence_quote: Guide: "The maximum duration of a Realtime session is 60 minutes." ... "Once the model has emitted audio in a session, the voice cannot be modified for that session." Developer notes blog (developers.openai.com/blog/realtime-api): "Realtime sessions can now last up to 60 minutes, up from 30 minutes." ... "The gpt-realtime model has a token window of 32,768 tokens. Responses can consume a maximum of 4,096 tokens. This means the model has a maximum input of 28,672 tokens." ... "The session instructions plus tools can have a maximum length of 16,384 tokens." ... "The service will automatically truncate (drop) messages when the session reaches 28,672 tokens, but this is configurable." ... "Set retention ratio to 0.8 ..." ... "You can disable this truncation behavior by setting \"truncation\": \"disabled\"" ... "When truncation alters the beginning of the conversation, it reduces the number of tokens that can be cached." Community thread (975036): {"type": "error", ... "error": {"type": "invalid_request_error", "code": "session_expired", "message": "Your session hit the maximum duration of 15 minutes." ...}} (Oct 2024) and "...maximum duration of 30 minutes." (Feb 2025); user: "Calling session.update regularly doesn't update the expiry time, it still stays at 15 mins from the session create time." Azure Q&A (26 Jan 2026): "The current maximum session duration for the Azure OpenAI Realtime API is indeed 30 minutes". CONTRADICTING — current Azure doc (learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/ai-foundry/openai/how-to/realtime-audio, ms.date 2026-07-29): "The maximum session duration is 60 minutes." and "Realtime sessions have a maximum duration of 60 minutes."
results.correction: (1) '30 on Azure' is stale: the Jan 2026 Azure Q&A did say 30 minutes, but the current Azure Realtime how-to (updated 2026-07-29) states the maximum session duration is 60 minutes. (2) The session_expired error code and its 'Your session hit the maximum duration of N minutes.' message are documented only in community/GitHub posts (observed with N=15 and N=30); no official OpenAI page found documents the code, and no post shows the 60-minute variant. (3) 'session.update does not extend the timer' rests on a single community user's Oct 2024 observation from the 15-minute era, not on official documentation. (4) The blog says truncation 'reduces the number of tokens that can be cached', a softer statement than 'busts the prompt cache'. (5) The token-window and truncation numbers come from the Developer-notes blog, not the realtime-conversations guide given as source_url. Corrected statement: 'OpenAI Realtime sessions max out at 60 minutes (Azure now also documents 60 minutes, up from 30 as of Jan 2026); expiry is reported (per community reports) as an error event with code session_expired, and developers report session.update does not reset expires_at; the gpt-realtime window is 32,768 tokens (4,096 max output, 28,672 max input, 16,384 for instructions+tools), and automatic truncation at 28,672 tokens reduces cacheable prefix tokens.'

sweeps.topic: Reference designs for interleaving tokens at different rates in one sequence (10 Hz act tokens, ~1 Hz language/plan lane, 12.5 Hz audio frames): fixed time blocks, chunk timelines with rate-limited channels, multi-stream delay lines, hold-last/cached slow features, spill queues, and frozen-prefix asynchronous chunk execution

findings.claim: ELLSA runs a single interleaved sequence on a fixed 1-second time block with the order speech -> image -> text -> action: `<bos>{5 speech embeddings}<eos><boi>{image tokens}<eoi><bot>{8 text tokens / <silence>}<eot><boa>{FAST action tokens / dummy action tokens}<eoa>`; rate mismatch is handled purely by fixed slots plus explicit idle tokens (<silence>, dummy actions). Two 8B experts need 786-854 ms per 1 s block on an A100; a 0.48 s block halves latency but the action expert loses 10-13 points because shorter action sequences 'reduce the temporal coherence of the generated actions'.
findings.source_title: End-to-end Listen, Look, Speak and Act (ELLSA), ICLR 2026

findings.numbers: 1 s block; speech 25 Hz -> 5 Hz (5 embeddings/block); 8 text tokens/block or <silence>; FAST action tokens for 1 s (0.48 s variant = 5 action frames/block, so ~10/s); TTS 25 codecs per 8 text embeddings (CosyVoice2-0.5B); LLaMA-3.1-8B + Emu3-Base, 32 layers/4096 each, LoRA r=256; latency A100: 854 ms S2S / 786 ms S2A at 1 s, 455 / 428 ms at 0.48 s; block ablation action expert LONG 94.0 -> 81.0 %, SPATIAL 95.4 -> 91.0 %; SA-MoE LONG 84.4 -> 71.6 %; dialogue turn-taking 100 % (Moshi 85.0), action turn-taking 96.4-100 %, interruptive-command barge-in 94.3 %, silence control 100 %; speaking-while-acting LIBERO LONG 84.4 -> 73.2 %, TriviaQA 45.2 -> 35.1; data ASR 481k, QA 728k, LIBERO 3,386 + 1,693 rejection; history: all speech/text, vision+action last 2 s
findings.relevance: Closest full precedent for Parcel Model A: language, vision, speech and ~10 Hz action tokens in one AR sequence; gives the block-size ablation and the A100 latency that rules out 8B-class models on Orin.

findings.claim: DuplexSLA decodes user audio, assistant speech and a rate-limited textual 'action channel' on one shared 160 ms chunk clock inside a single token stream: `<|user_audio_begin|> U U <|user_audio_end|> <|assistant_audio_begin|> T A A A A <|assistant_audio_end|> {<=10 action tokens} <|action_end|>`. Idle chunks emit <vad_silence>/<tts_pad> anchors and always the <|action_end|> marker ('keeps every chunk strictly aligned to the 160 ms clock'); the <=10-token cap is 'a deployment budget, not an architectural constraint' chosen so decoding fits the chunk on the accelerator, and overflow spills FIFO into later chunks without splitting a tool-call block or blocking speech.
findings.source_title: DuplexSLA: A Full-Duplex Spoken Language Model with Synchronized Speech, Language, and Action
findings.kind: arxiv-paper (CC BY 4.0; PDF text-extracted; github.com/hyzhang24/DuplexSLA MIT badge, weights 'coming soon'; project page hyzhang24.github.io/DuplexSLA)
findings.numbers: 7B backbone from Step-Audio 2 mini (HTML summarizer once returned '77B' - parse artifact; PDF table and README say 7B); 160 ms chunk; user 2 causal features x 80 ms; assistant TA4 = 1 text anchor + 4 audio tokens at 40 ms; action channel <=10 tokens/chunk (<=62.5 tok/s); user-transcript lag 2 chunks = 320 ms; turn-taking accuracy/delay (context prefill): normal 96.00 % / 0.27 s, pause 93.33 % / 0.27 s, interrupt 99.33 % / 0.40 s, backchannel 98.33 % / 0.32 s; tool calling 85.56 % at 0.64 s avg (~4x lower than ASR+LLM cascade); CPT ~500k h audio (320k h duplex, 2x90k h ASR) + 1.92M text; post-train ~50k h; DuplexSLA-Bench 2,100 cases; 50 function schemas
findings.relevance: Exact template for Parcel: a capped, time-stamped text lane (plan/steering/receipts) interleaved with high-rate tokens, with a hardware-derived budget and spill queue; also the precedent for Model B steering injection labels (interrupt/backchannel/response) at 0.3-0.4 s.

findings.claim: Moshi reconciles ~3-4 text tokens/s with 12.5 Hz audio by padding the text stream with PAD/EPAD tokens (about 65 % of text slots) and decoding 17 parallel streams per 80 ms frame (1 text + 8 own audio + 8 user audio) with a 7B Temporal Transformer plus a small Depth Transformer; inter-stream delays are the control knob: acoustic delay 2 frames in pretraining and 1 in fine-tuning (160 ms theoretical latency), text delay 0 for dialogue, and a 2 s text or audio delay turns the same model into streaming ASR or TTS.
findings.source_title: Moshi: a speech-text foundation model for real-time dialogue
findings.kind: arxiv-paper (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; PDF text-extracted; code github.com/kyutai-labs/moshi)
findings.numbers: Mimi 24 kHz -> 12.5 Hz, 80 ms frame, Q=8 x 2048, 1.1 kbps; K=2Q+1=17 streams; Temporal 7B (32 layers, 4096, 32 heads), Depth 6 layers/1024/16 heads; 3-4 text tokens/s; PAD ~65 % of text tokens; Table 1: pretrain acoustic delay 2, text delay +/-0.6 s randomized; finetune acoustic delay 1, text delay 0; Table 6 delay [0,2,2,2,2,2,2,2] + RQ perplexity 36.8 vs [0,1..7] 40.3 vs no-RQ 135.4; ASR: text delayed 2 s, tau=2; TTS: audio delayed 2 s; latency 160 ms theoretical, 200 ms on L4; data 7M h + Fisher 2000 h + 170 h + >20k h synthetic; when silent: PAD text + natural-silence audio
findings.relevance: Canonical 'pad the slow stream to the fast clock' and 'delay line' designs; shows audio at 12.5 Hz belongs in parallel streams decoded by a depth transformer, not interleaved tokens.

findings.claim: Delayed Streams Modeling generalizes Moshi's trick: any set of time-aligned streams on a 12.5 Hz grid with per-stream integer delays; 'ASR corresponds to the text stream being delayed, while the opposite gives a text-to-speech model'. STT delay is a tunable 0.25-4 s knob with measured WER cost, TTS delays audio 16 steps (1.28 s), and an extra control stream predicts whether the next input text token is a WORD, i.e. a learned 'is there new slow-lane content' signal.
findings.source_title: Streaming Sequence-to-Sequence Learning with Delayed Streams Modeling (Kyutai)
findings.numbers: 12.5 Hz grid; text PAD/WORD tokens; STT delays 0.25-4 s, default 2.5 s, latency precision ~300 ms; WER 6.4 % short-form (9 sets), 7.9 % long-form; Fig. 4 WER ~7 % at 0.25 s -> ~5.5 % at 4 s; STT 2.6B (2048 dim, 48 layers) and 300M; TTS audio delay 1.28 s = 16 steps, first audio 150 ms (batch 1), 380/403 ms at batch 32/64, 1.8B (1B + 0.8B RQ sampler); lookahead text stream l=2
findings.relevance: Gives the quantitative latency-vs-quality curve for a delay line and a precedent for an explicit 'new plan token arriving' stream for Model A's plan lane.

findings.claim: Hibiki applies the multistream design to simultaneous translation: source audio, target audio and target text streams at 12.5 Hz with an acoustic delay of 2 steps and a learned per-word lag of at least 2 s derived from translation-model perplexity; a 1.7B distilled variant runs faster than real time on an iPhone 16 Pro.
findings.source_title: High-Fidelity Simultaneous Speech-To-Speech Translation (Hibiki), ICML 2025
findings.numbers: 12.5 Hz; up to 16 quantizers per stream; acoustic delay 2 steps; target lags >=2 s vs contextual alignment (MADLAD-3B); Temporal 2.2B (24 layers, 20 heads, local attention 500 tokens, 40 s context); Depth 1.1B (6 layers/codebook) or 449M distilled; Hibiki 2.7B, Hibiki-M 1.7B on-device; 320 parallel sequences faster than real time on H100; ASR-BLEU 39.2 vs Seamless 37.0 (short), 27.5 vs 25.4 (long); speaker sim 0.41/0.48; MOS 3.73 vs 2.18; LAAL 5.0 s; ~40K h per language, 900 h synthetic
findings.relevance: Shows a multi-stream depth-transformer model of ~1.7B running real-time on a phone-class chip, a data point for what stream count and size fit an edge budget.

findings.claim: RT-H puts a language-motion token sequence between task and action using one PaLI-X 55B VLM queried twice per step, and removes the doubled latency by predicting the language motion one step ahead so both queries batch: 'we query the action using the inferred language motion of the previous time step, while also predicting the language motion for the next time step ... nearly identical querying lag as RT-2'. Humans intervene by typing a replacement language motion that is fed straight into the action query.
findings.source_title: RT-H: Action Hierarchies Using Language, RSS 2024
findings.numbers: PaLI-X 55B; >2500 auto-labelled language motions; 100K demos (70K Kitchen + 30K Diverse); +15 % over RT-2 on 8 tasks; RT-H-Intervene 60-70 % improvement on precise tasks vs RT-2-IWR; no ms latency reported
findings.relevance: The 'predict-ahead by one block' mechanism is the cheapest way to keep Parcel's ~1 Hz plan lane from stalling the 10 Hz act lane, and the typed language-motion correction is a precedent for owner steering injection.

findings.claim: pi0.5 runs a two-stage inference in one model: first a high-level text subtask, then 50 Hz action chunks from a flow-matching expert conditioned on it; the paper states only that 'the high-level inference process still runs at a lower frequency than low-level action inference' (rate unspecified) and that pre-training uses discrete FAST action tokens while post-training adds the continuous expert with alpha = 10.
findings.source_title: pi0.5: a Vision-Language-Action Model with Open-World Generalization
findings.kind: arxiv-paper (arXiv perpetual license; blog only, no weights)
findings.numbers: 50 Hz with action chunking; 10 denoising steps; alpha = 10.0; 280k pre-train + 80k post-train steps; ~400 h mobile-manipulator data over ~100 homes; 97.6 % of first-phase data not from mobile manipulators; tasks 2-5 min in 3 unseen homes; language following ~60-70 % ID / ~40-50 % OOD (Fig. 9); bidirectional attention among image/text/continuous-action tokens, action representations do not attend to each other
findings.relevance: Discrete-then-continuous is the standard recipe; confirms the subtask lane is held across many action chunks but leaves the refresh rate unmeasured (open item for Parcel).

findings.claim: SmolVLA's asynchronous stack decouples chunk prediction from execution with a queue: the client requests a new chunk when the remaining actions fall below a fraction g of chunk size n, merges overlapping timesteps by aggregation, and skips near-duplicate observations; the LeRobot blog recommends g~0.7 and reports ~2x faster task completion.
findings.source_title: SmolVLA: A Vision-Language-Action Model for Affordable and Efficient Robotics (+ LeRobot async blog)
findings.numbers: 450M params (~100M action expert, first 16 LLM layers); flow matching 10 steps; chunk n=50; trigger |A_t|/n < g, blog: g~0.7 (start 0.5); aggregators Replace / Weighted blend; joint-space near-duplicate skip eps; async task 9.7 s vs 13.75 s sync (~30 % faster), 19 vs 9 pick-place cycles; blog: ~100 ms (ACT on 2021 MacBook Pro), sub-100 ms round trip with SmolVLA on RTX 4090, ~2x speedup; LIBERO 87.3 %, SO100 78.3 %; ~30k GPU hours
findings.relevance: The size class (0.45B) and the simplest hold-last chunk queue Parcel can copy for the act-token lane; the g threshold is the tunable that hides one block of decode latency.

findings.claim: Real-Time Chunking makes chunked policies robust to inference delay by freezing the first d = floor(delta/dt) actions of the next chunk and inpainting the rest via guidance; with pi0.5 at 50 Hz (H = 50) and d up to 16 (320 ms) real bimanual tasks show 'no degradation, whereas synchronous degrades linearly', at +21 ms overhead.
findings.source_title: Real-Time Execution of Action Chunking Flow Policies (RTC), NeurIPS 2025
findings.numbers: H=50 at 50 Hz (dt=20 ms, 1 s lookahead); base 76 ms on RTX 4090, RTC +21 ms = 97 ms; remote baseline d~6; +100/+200 ms injected -> d~11/16; guidance weight 1 on frozen prefix, exponential decay over overlap, 0 on last s; 12 Kinetix tasks + 6 real bimanual (match lighting); temporal ensembling 'poor actions', naive async 'jerky, out-of-distribution', bidirectional decoding 2.3x latency
findings.relevance: The delay-handling rule for Parcel's act lane: with one block of decode latency at 10 Hz (d=1-2), a frozen-prefix scheme is proven far beyond that range.

findings.claim: A 2026 controlled comparison of asynchronous VLA inference (IT-RTC, TT-RTC, VLASH, A2C2) at 50 Hz finds that inference-time inpainting collapses to the naive baseline beyond d = 8 on long (H = 50) chunks, while a per-step residual correction head (A2C2, +1.8 % compute) leads from d = 4 onward; training-time delay simulation (TT-RTC) is 'essentially free' with a generous d_max.
findings.source_title: Understanding Asynchronous Inference Methods for Vision-Language-Action Models
findings.numbers: 50 Hz, dt=20 ms; Kinetix H in {16,30}, d<=15 (300 ms); LIBERO SmolVLA H=50, d<=20; cloud-over-4G d=13, edge-over-4G d=3; Kinetix H=16: A2C2 >90 % at d=8, naive <40 %; LIBERO: A2C2 ~10-point margin from d=4, IT-RTC ~naive beyond d=8, VLASH ~55-56 % through d=20; RTX 3090: IT-RTC 469.7 ms (+15.9 %, 2.13 Hz), TT-RTC 402.7 ms, A2C2 412.4 ms (+1.8 %)
findings.relevance: Tells Parcel which async mechanism to pick as a function of measured block latency d on the Orin, and that training with simulated staleness is nearly free.

findings.claim: Fast-in-Slow embeds System 1 in the last two transformer blocks of a 7B VLM and runs it at a fixed integer ratio to System 2; ablating ratios 1:1 to 1:8 finds 1:4 best, and with an action chunk of 8 it reaches 117.7 Hz on an RTX 4090 (21.9 Hz at chunk 1), i.e. hold-last of the slow latent for exactly four fast steps is the sweet spot.
findings.source_title: Fast-in-Slow: A Dual-System Foundation Model Unifying Fast Manipulation within Slow Reasoning, NeurIPS 2025
findings.numbers: LLaMA2-7B; System 1 = final 2 blocks; System-2:System-1 ratio 1:1..1:8, best 1:4; 117.7 Hz (chunk 8) / 21.9 Hz (chunk 1) on RTX 4090; 2x CogACT 9.8 Hz; RLBench 69 % (+8 vs CogACT, +14 vs pi0); Agilex 68 % vs pi0 59, AlphaBot 74 % vs 61; 860K trajectories; 8 A800, 300 epochs
findings.relevance: Direct evidence on how stale a slow lane may be before performance drops (1:4 good, 1:8 worse) - the ratio Parcel's 10 Hz / ~1-2 Hz split should be tested against.

findings.claim: UniFS names the 'frequency dilemma' of fast-slow systems ('large update gaps cause semantic drift from stale context, while small gaps erode the intended computational savings') and answers it with one 0.5B VLM stratified into five layer groups recomputed at timescales [1, 2, 4, 8, 16] with cached features in between, giving the action expert multi-timescale latents at 17.8 ms average latency.
findings.source_title: UniFS: Unified Fast-to-Slow Hierarchical Architecture for Vision-Language-Action Models
findings.numbers: Qwen2.5-0.5B + DINOv2/SigLIP; 5 groups, timescales [1,2,4,8,16], group k recomputes if t = 0 mod n_k; action expert 24 layers, 7-DoF; latency 17.8 ms avg (12.3-32.6) vs 36.5 ms VLA-Adapter; theoretical 2.6x speedup; LIBERO 98.3 % (Spatial 99.6, Object 99.6, Goal 98.1, Long 95.6) vs 95.8 %; 4 A100 training
findings.relevance: A small-model design where the rate hierarchy lives inside one network's layers rather than in separate models - the size and latency class that could plausibly hit 10 Hz on Orin.

findings.claim: TIDAL is the only edge measurement in this set: on a Jetson AGX Orin (Max-N, TensorRT) a 3B GR00T-N1.5 goes from ~2.4 Hz to ~9 Hz by freezing high-level intent over a 16-step horizon and interleaving single-step Euler denoising with execution of 4 actions at a time, at the cost of an 8-point drop on static tasks.
findings.source_title: TIDAL: Temporally Interleaved Diffusion and Action Loop for High-Frequency VLA Control
findings.numbers: GR00T-N1.5-3B; Jetson AGX Orin Max-N TensorRT; H=16, N=4 executed per micro-loop, K=4 latency stages; ~110 ms vs ~400 ms cycle; ~9 Hz vs ~2.4 Hz; dynamic interception 0.61/0.36 vs 0.31/0.16; RoboCasa static 50.94 % vs 59.25 %; non-paused inference 0.30 vs 0.09; no real-robot results yet
findings.relevance: Sets the realistic Orin budget: even a 3B diffusion VLA needs interleaving tricks to approach 10 Hz, so Parcel's 10 Hz lane must be a small act-token head with language on the slow lane.

findings.claim: OneTwoVLA switches between reasoning and acting inside one sequence with [BOR]/[BOA] tokens: reasoning text is generated only at key moments and then stays in context ('the latest reasoning content R') while actions are decoded, so total wall time matches a flat pi0; new human input is handled by appending the interaction text to the instruction for subsequent steps.
findings.source_title: OneTwoVLA: A Unified Vision-Language-Action Model with Adaptive Reasoning, ICLR 2026
findings.numbers: tokens [BOR], [BOA]; base pi0; long-horizon 87 % vs pi0 30 %; error recovery 8/10 vs 8/14; human interaction 20/20; visual grounding 78 % vs 5 %; 16,000 synthetic reasoning samples (6,000 grounding + 10,000 planning, Gemini 2.5 Pro + FLUX.1-dev); no ms latency given
findings.relevance: The event-triggered alternative to a fixed-slot plan lane, and the simplest steering-injection precedent (append owner text to the instruction) for Model B.

findings.claim: MiniCPM-o 4.5's Omni-Flow interleaves perception and generation in fixed time windows, and its ablation picks 1.0 s as the best window ('0.2 s, 0.1 s caused significant performance degradation'); within each window the layout is [visual ; audio ; output] with a [listen] token when silent, input audio compressed to 10 tokens/s, text decoded at 3-4 steps/s and ~25 tok/s speech kept out of the LLM in a light decoder.
findings.source_title: MiniCPM-o 4.5: Towards Real-Time Full-Duplex Omni-Modal Interaction (+ MiniCPM-o 2.6 model card, Apache-2.0)
findings.numbers: window t = 1.0 s best; 0.2 s / 0.1 s degrade; g_k = [v^k ; a^k ; o^k]; audio 50 tok/s (Whisper medium 0.3B) -> 10 tok/s; text 3-4 decoding steps/s; speech ~25 tok/s via ~0.3B decoder + flow-matching vocoder; [listen] token; 9B total on Qwen3-8B; RTF 0.27 on RTX 4090 BF16, 0.21 INT4; <12 GB RAM; first-token 0.59 s with 64 frames; LiveSports-3K-CC 54.4 vs 41.5/45.6; 2.6: TDM 'small periodic time slices', 8B, Apache-2.0
findings.relevance: Independent confirmation (with ELLSA) that ~1 s is the block size that works for perception-generation interleaving, and that audio generation should be a side decoder rather than LLM tokens.

findings.claim: Chain-of-Action orders action tokens within one autoregressive trajectory goal-first: 'the first token corresponds to a stable keyframe action that encodes the task-specific goals, and subsequent action tokens are generated autoregressively' backward toward the current state, with multi-token prediction and dynamic stopping; it carries no language tokens and runs at 10 Hz on a laptop 4070 over a 1000 Hz PD loop.
findings.source_title: Chain-of-Action: Trajectory Autoregressive Modeling for Robotic Manipulation, NeurIPS 2025
findings.kind: arxiv-paper (project page chain-of-action.github.io; license not stated)
findings.numbers: continuous action tokens; MTP 5 heads; reverse temporal ensemble; 10 Hz policy on 4070 laptop, PD 1000 Hz; RLBench-60 0.552 vs ACT 0.389 vs DP 0.326 (+16.3 / +23.2 pts); real 8 kitchen tasks 0.613 vs 0.463 (+15 %); ResNet-18 + 4-layer enc / 7-layer dec, d=512, 8 heads
findings.relevance: A coarse-to-fine ordering of act tokens (goal token first) that could occupy the first act slot of each Parcel block; it shows 10 Hz AR action decoding is feasible for a small model but not with language in the loop.

design_implications: Choose a block that is an integer multiple of every native rate and make the token layout the clock: 10 Hz act (100 ms), 12.5 Hz audio (80 ms) and ~1 Hz plan have LCM 400 ms, so one block = 4 act tokens + 5 audio features + a capped plan slot + a mandatory block-end marker (DuplexSLA's <|action_end|> rule); ELLSA had to fall back to 0.48 s because 25 Hz speech cannot make 0.5 s, and 12.5 Hz cannot make 1 s (12.5 frames).

Fill every block, never skip a lane: every single-backbone multi-rate system emits an explicit idle token (ELLSA <silence> + dummy actions, DuplexSLA <vad_silence>/<tts_pad>, Moshi PAD at 65 %, MiniCPM-o [listen]); Model A's plan lane should emit a <hold> token per block so the 10 Hz act lane never waits on the slow lane.

Cap the plan/steering lane by measured Orin decode budget and spill FIFO (DuplexSLA: 'a deployment budget, not an architectural constraint ... re-tuned per accelerator without retraining'): tokens/s of the backbone on Orin minus the act tokens per block, with margin; overflow continues in later blocks without splitting a structured receipt.

Do not plan on an 8B-class interleaved model at 10 Hz on Orin: ELLSA (2x8B) needs 786-854 ms per 1 s block on an A100; TIDAL's 3B GR00T-N1.5 reaches only ~9 Hz on Orin with a 4-of-16 interleaving trick and an 8-point static-task penalty. The size class with a chance is 0.45-0.5B (SmolVLA, UniFS 17.8 ms on a data-center GPU); the 10 Hz lane must be a small act-token head with language on the slow lane.

Use a one-block delay line for the plan lane (RT-H predict-one-step-ahead; Moshi/DSM delays): decode the plan for block t+1 during block t so act tokens never stall; for Model B receipts use DuplexSLA's 2-chunk (320 ms) delayed transcript channel as the precedent for time-stamped narration text that never blocks speech.

Hold-last is the default for stale plans but must be trained for: HiRT trains on randomly stale latents, FiS finds 1:4 optimal and 1:8 worse, UniFS names 'semantic drift from stale context'; if the plan refreshes every ~10 act tokens, train with randomized 5-20-token staleness and measure drift.

Model B steering injection: copy DuplexSLA's action-channel labels (interrupt/backchannel/response at 0.27-0.40 s while speech continues) and OneTwoVLA's 'append interaction text to the instruction'; owner speech becomes a short steering string in the next block's plan slot, never in the act tokens, with ELLSA's 'Action Cancelled' barge-in (94.3 %) as the safety path.

Async execution of act chunks: adopt a frozen-prefix scheme and measure d in blocks; RTC shows no degradation to d=16 at 50 Hz (+21 ms), the 2026 survey says beyond d=4 a per-step correction head (A2C2, +1.8 % compute) beats inpainting and IT-RTC collapses beyond d=8, and training-time delay simulation is nearly free; REALFAST's 183-302 ms bound for m=4-6 AR tokens is the closest token-decoding analogue.

Keep 12.5 Hz audio out of the interleaved token stream: Moshi/Hibiki/DSM decode 17 streams per frame with a depth transformer, Qwen3-Omni runs an asynchronously prefilled Talker, MiniCPM-o 4.5 keeps 25 tok/s speech in a side decoder; since Parcel's voice is the hosted Realtime model, Model A should ingest at most 12.5 Hz features (5 per 400 ms block) and never generate audio tokens.

Block-size evidence to carry into the design review: 1 s is the empirical sweet spot for perception-generation interleaving (ELLSA 1 s vs 0.48 s: action expert LONG 94.0 -> 81.0 %; MiniCPM-o 4.5: 1.0 s best, 0.2/0.1 s degrade), 160 ms works for speech-only duplex with a 7B model (DuplexSLA), and no paper ablates fixed-slot vs event-triggered slow lanes at equal compute (ELLSA vs OneTwoVLA are the two poles).
