results.correction: Architecture, single-MLP goal/embodiment tokens, S formula, 100 runs/env, Ouster OS1-32 on a Husky, 2x body scaling and the real-robot 85% vs 15% are all exact. The two summary percentages are not: masking LiDAR drops SR 0.79->0.17, 0.61->0.37, 0.76->0.20, i.e. relative losses of 78%/39%/74% (mean SR 0.72 -> 0.25, roughly two-thirds lost, not 'about half'); masking images gives 0.72/0.67/0.23, i.e. -9% in Env 1, +10% in Env 2 (image masking IMPROVED SR there) and -70% in Env 3 (nearly as bad as LiDAR masking), so 'costs 10-30%' holds only as a three-env average (~25%) and hides that in one environment images were as load-bearing as LiDAR. Corrected statement: 'masking LiDAR loses 39-78% of SR (mean ~66%); masking images ranges from a 10% gain to a 70% loss (mean ~25%)'. Minor: the paper's title is 'Multimodal embodiment-aware navigation transformer' (ViLiNT is the model name, not in the title); the number of real-world trials behind 85%/15% is not stated.

results.claim: A transformer over 360-degree LiDAR ray tokens (180 rays x 15 history frames, from a 30x180 spherical depth image) plus proprioception runs at 50 Hz in ~1.3 ms on a Unitree Go2 with Livox Mid-360 and Jetson AGX Orin 64 GB, beside PPO locomotion, safety-shield and navigation policies, with zero real-world collisions.
results.evidence_quote: "Each frame of points is first downsampled using a spherical grid ... This yields a 30×180 circular depth image per frame ... We accumulate the past 15 frames as input to a shared 1D-CNN, which compresses the channel dimension (30→16) for each frame. In parallel, an MLP encodes the past 15 proprioceptive measurements ... producing a 16-d feature for each frame ... The LiDAR and proprioceptive features of all frames are then concatenated along the channel dimension at each spatial location to form tokens, which are subsequently fed into a Transformer encoder (with learnable temporal encodings applied to distinguish historical frames). Finally, the fused tokens are processed through a 1D U-Net to generate the final ray-based representation." ... "both safety-shield and navigation policies take the same exteroception represented by 180 equidistant rays covering a 360° FoV, which are predicted by the exteroceptive estimator from raw LiDAR scans." ... "All modules maintain stable real-time performance at 50 Hz over 60 s"; estimator inference "1.3±0.1 ms" (Table III). "Unitree Go2 robot equipped with a Livox Mid-360 LiDAR and a Jetson AGX Orin (64 GB)". Real-world Static 270 s / Dynamic 180 s / DeadEnd 190 s / Herding 93 s: "the robot exhibits no collisions with any obstacle". Table I training: Locomotion 4 h/15 GB, Safety-Shield 15 h/12 GB, Navigation 7 h/15 GB, Estimator ~10 h/12 GB.
results.correction: Hardware, 50 Hz, ~1.3 ms (estimator-only inference time), PPO locomotion/safety-shield/navigation modules, and zero real-world collisions are all confirmed verbatim. The token description is off: the transformer does not attend over '180 rays x 15 frames' ray tokens. Its input tokens are the 180 azimuth columns of the 30x180 depth image (one token per spatial location), each formed by concatenating the 15 frames' 1D-CNN LiDAR features (16-d) and proprio MLP features (16-d) along the channel dimension, with learnable temporal encodings; the '180 equidistant rays' are the estimator's OUTPUT (via a 1D U-Net) consumed by the policies, not its input tokens. Corrected: 'a transformer over 180 azimuth-column tokens (15 frames x 32-d stacked per token) built from 15 frames of a 30x180 spherical depth image plus proprioception, outputting 180 rays'. Metadata note: VRAM is 15/12/15/12 GB per module, not a flat 12 GB.

results.claim: For VLM-based navigators, a raw obstacle/occupancy map image is worth nothing, but an annotated semantic map (text labels at region centroids) rendered as one SigLIP image replaces the whole frame history: SR rises from 27.3 (no map) to 36.5, memory is a constant 0.17 MB instead of 276 MB at 300 steps, and inference drops 79.5%.
results.evidence_quote: Table 4 "Comparison of different map representation methods" (NE/OS/SR/SPL): MapNav (w/o Map) 7.26/41.2/27.3/23.2; MapNav (Original Map) 8.93/35.1/26.4/21.9; MapNav (Semantic Map) 6.56/43.2/29.1/24.5; MapNav (ASM) 5.22/50.3/36.5/34.3 — where Original Map is "the original top-down map from the simulator" and Semantic Map is "a semantic map with categorical information but no textual annotations". "we introduce MapNav, a novel end-to-end VLN model that leverages Annotated Semantic Map (ASM) to replace historical frames". "For each semantic region exceeding the minimum area threshold τ, we compute its geometric centroid to establish a text anchor point". "the observation frame produces X_t ... Similarly, the ASM generates X_t^M" through the shared SigLIP encoder ("SigLIP-so400m-patch14-384", LLM "Qwen2-7B-Instruct", LLaVA-OneVision). "MapNav reduces average processing time by 79.5% (from 1.22 seconds per step to 0.25 seconds)". "maintains a constant memory footprint of 0.17MB, regardless of trajectory length, while Navid's frame-based approach scales linearly, reaching 276MB at 300 steps". Venue: ACL Anthology 2025.acl-long.638, Proceedings of the 63rd ACL (Long Papers), pp. 13032-13056.
results.correction: No correction to the claim text: the raw simulator top-down map is slightly worse than no map on every metric (26.4 vs 27.3 SR), ASM + current RGB only (no history) reaches 36.5, and the memory/inference figures are verbatim. Two metadata notes: (1) the ASM-only row (36.5) is still below NaVid-all-frames (37.4); the config that beats NaVid (39.7/37.2) adds the current RGB plus 2 history frames, so 'replaces the whole frame history' is the paper's framing rather than the SOTA-beating config; (2) the 'RxR-CE zero-shot 32.6/27.7 vs 23.8/21.2' in the numbers field is mislabeled — that MapNav row is trained on R2R+RxR; the R2R-only zero-shot row is 22.1/20.2 vs NaVid 13.0/7.8.

results.claim: Direct speech tokens (Whisper encoder -> ~300 tokens per utterance projected into the LLM) match text instructions and beat an ASR cascade by 5-18 points on chained manipulation tasks, and the speaker's voice enables owner-specific tasks at 86.5% vs 19.2% for a text VLA.
results.evidence_quote: "the speech signal is first transformed into an 80-bin mel-spectrogram ... padded to a fixed length of 3000 frames. The speech encoder processes this mel-spectrogram and produces a sequence of 1500 hidden representations" ... "we apply a simple reshape operation along the time dimension, using a reduction factor of 5" -> 300 speech tokens -> MLP projector. Table 1 (CALVIN LH-1..LH-5, Avg.Len): VLA+ (text) 95.5/85.0/74.9/66.8/58.2, 3.80; VLAS* (synthetic speech) 94.2/84.0/73.2/64.3/54.6, 3.70; VLAS* (real speech) 93.6/82.8/71.6/61.4/51.3, 3.61; VLA*+ASR (Whisper large-v2 cascade, synthetic speech from "39 novel voices") 88.7/74.1/61.0/49.2/40.2, 3.13. Legend: "+: Evaluated with the ground truth textual instructions. *: Evaluated with the speech instructions." Table 2 Avg: VLA+ 19.2%; VLAS* 86.5%; VLAS*(Real) 78.6%; VLAS*-RAG 16.0%; VLA++RAG 82.0%. RAG: "the raw speech command is processed by the speaker identification module to extract a voiceprint. This voiceprint serves as a key to query an external database"; retrieved info is "integrated as background knowledge and passed to the LLM, in conjunction with visual and speech tokens." SQA: "185K SQA samples ... over 1,152 different voices"; CSI: "approximately 194K audio samples".
results.correction: Whisper -> 300 tokens, near-parity with text (within 1.3-3.6 points), and 86.5% vs 19.2% are exact. The '5-18 points over the ASR cascade' is wrong: comparing VLAS with synthetic speech against VLA*+ASR under the same synthetic-speech condition gives +5.5/+9.9/+12.2/+15.1/+14.4 on LH-1..5, i.e. 5-15 points (4.9-12.2 with real speech). The 18-point figure is the TEXT VLA's LH-5 margin over the cascade (58.2-40.2), not a speech-token model's. Corrected: 'beat an ASR cascade by 5-15 points'. Also, the paper's mechanism for owner-specific tasks is a separate pre-trained voiceprint extractor whose lookup result is fed to the LLM as text background knowledge (RAG), not a voice embedding token — VLAS without RAG scores 16.0%, and a text-only VLA given the same RAG scores 82.0%, so identity retrieval, not the speech tokens themselves, accounts for almost all of the 86.5%.

sweeps.topic: On-device owner-voice (speaker) verification and robot-directed-speech / addressee gating for a household robot, incl. how hosted voice APIs gate barge-in on addressee

findings.claim: Wake-word-free, audio-only device-addressed speech detection runs on ARM Cortex-A72 (no GPU) in a 3-stage cascade (beamformer -> ~435K-param log-mel classifier -> ~85K-param causal Transformer over an 8 s rolling context); the 8 s interaction-state stage is the largest contributor (removing it drops F1 by 38 points). Weights are not released; corpus is proprietary.
findings.source_title: Selective Attention System (SAS): Device-Addressed Speech Detection for Real-Time On-Device Voice AI (Attention Labs)
findings.kind: arXiv preprint (internal evaluation, no third-party audit)
findings.numbers: ~520K params total, <20 MB runtime; audio-only at tau=0.70: F1 0.86 (P 0.89 / R 0.83), false-trigger 2.1% (7.8% with TV audio), single-mic fallback F1 0.84; audio+video F1 0.95 (P 0.97 / R 0.93); latency audio-only median 38 ms / p95 51 ms, A+V median 105 ms / p95 142 ms on Cortex-A72, also RPi 4 and Reachy Mini; ablation: no Stage 3 -> F1 0.57±0.03; 600 h corpus, 60 h test, 1-4 speakers, 28-85 dBA; test mix ~34% silence / ~58% person-directed / ~8% device-directed
findings.relevance: Direct template for Parcel's pre-ASR addressee gate on the Orin: shape, size, expected false-trigger rate and the necessity of interaction-state context.

findings.claim: The best published EER for device-directed speech detection without a wake word combines ASR 1-best text, acoustic embeddings and ASR decoder signals in an LLM; audio-only or text-only alone are ~11-13% EER, so a pre-ASR acoustic gate is necessary but not sufficient.
findings.source_title: A Multimodal Approach to Device-Directed Speech Detection with Large Language Models (Apple, ICASSP 2024)
findings.numbers: GPT-2 124.4M: text-only 12.70% EER, audio-only Whisper 10.98%, CLAP 19.13%, decoder-signals-only 28.09%; multimodal MM6 7.95% (Whisper) / 7.45% (CLAP) = 27.6-61.1% rel. over audio-only, 34.6-38.7% over text-only; GPT-2 1.5B + Whisper, LoRA r=64: 6.53%; train ~40k DD (~59 h) + ~40k ND (~67 h) + ~3M text utterances; eval ~14k DD / ~23k ND (~35 h); Whisper 769M, CLAP 153M
findings.relevance: Sets the accuracy floor Parcel's Stage-C (text + prosody + confidence) addressee confirmation should be measured against, and the data volume needed (~80k labelled utterances).

findings.claim: For follow-up turns without a wake word, jointly modelling the previous dialogue context and ASR n-best uncertainty roughly halves false accepts at a fixed 10% false-reject rate.
findings.source_title: Device-Directed Speech Detection for Follow-up Conversations Using Large Language Models (Apple)
findings.numbers: ~245k follow-up segments from ~19k recordings / 1.3k participants, DD:ND ~1:4, 3.5±3.25 s; Vicuna-7B + LoRA 4.1M params (0.06%) + ~8k head; at 10% FRR: follow-up only 1-best EER 10.5% / FAR 11.4%; 8-best 9.5% / 8.3%; +context 1-best 8.5% / 6.1%; +context +8-best 7.9% / 4.8% ("~20-40% reduction in FAR"); inference on 4x A100
findings.relevance: Justifies keeping an 8-10 s conversational state (robot just spoke / owner just addressed it) as an input to Parcel's gate, and an n-best-aware ASR interface in the language lane.

findings.claim: An acoustics-only DDSD model of ~4.8M parameters (6 self-attention layers over 40-D mel at 100 fps) reaches 6.2% EER after distillation from an ASR-lattice teacher and can be deployed where ASR cannot; an ensemble with the ASR-based model reaches 4.0%.
findings.source_title: Device-Directed Speech Detection: Regularization via Distillation for Weakly-Supervised Models (Apple, Interspeech 2022)
findings.numbers: AFTM ~4.8M params, 6 SA layers x 4 heads, 40-D mel @ 100 fps; EER: base 18.4% -> distilled 6.2% ("66% gain"); LatticeRNN 4.8%; ensemble 4.0% ("20%" further)
findings.relevance: Evidence that a small pre-ASR acoustic gate on the Orin can reach single-digit EER if distilled from a text-aware teacher, rather than trained from weak labels alone.

findings.claim: Amazon's camera+mic Conversation Mode detects device-directed speech without a wake word via an on-device fusion of a head-orientation model and a separable-CNN acoustic model; the fusion sharply reduces false rejects and false wakes, including wakes triggered by the device's own TTS.
findings.source_title: New Alexa feature enables natural, multiparty interactions (Amazon Science blog)
findings.numbers: visual head-orientation model reduced FRR "by almost 80%"; adding audio reduced FRR "by 83% relative to a model that used visual data only"; "80% reduction in false wakes due to ambient noise and a 42% reduction in false wakes triggered by Alexa's own responses"; entered by voice command, exits on inactivity
findings.relevance: Shows the barge-in gate must consume the robot's own TTS as context and that head-pose toward the robot is the strongest single cue; also the 'explicit enter/exit conversation mode' pattern.

findings.claim: Hosted voice APIs do not solve addressee for the robot: OpenAI Realtime offers only server_vad / semantic_vad plus interrupt/create flags with no documented option to ignore speech not directed at the model; Gemini Live's proactive_audio (model 'can proactively decide not to respond if the content is not relevant') is available only on the 2.5 Flash Live preview and is not supported on Gemini 3.1 Flash Live.
findings.source_title: Gemini Live API capabilities guide (Proactive audio) — cross-checked with OpenAI Realtime VAD guide https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/realtime-vad
findings.numbers: Gemini: proactivity.proactive_audio=true, v1beta, 2.5 Flash Live Preview only, 'not supported in Gemini 3.1 Flash Live'; VAD params start_of_speech_sensitivity / end_of_speech_sensitivity / prefix_padding_ms / silence_duration_ms; on interruption 'ongoing generation is canceled and discarded'. OpenAI: server_vad (threshold, prefix_padding_ms, silence_duration_ms), semantic_vad eagerness low/medium/high/auto, create_response / interrupt_response; no addressee gate.
findings.relevance: Model B must gate audio locally (owner + addressee) before any bytes are forwarded to the hosted OpenAI Realtime voice; there is no server-side fallback.

findings.claim: On a social robot in real multi-party rooms, cloud voice-based speaker identification was nearly useless while face recognition and gaze-based turn-taking carried addressee detection; the system was ~92% correct on addressee with two parallel dyads and ~79% in a group, at ~1.35 s latency.
findings.source_title: Multi-party open-ended conversation with a social robot (Frontiers in Robotics and AI; Furhat, 30 participants)
findings.numbers: Azure speaker ID correct 18.4% (group) / 26.8% (parallel); face recognition 80.0% / 94.7%; addressee correct 92.6% (parallel) / 79.3% (group), incorrect 7.0% / 13.6%; response latency 1.35 s (SD 0.55), up to ~5 s; ReSpeaker DOA + GPT-3.5; 30 participants (8F/22M); turn taken 'if the robot is looked at by the last speaker or after prolonged silence'
findings.relevance: Strongest in-the-wild evidence that owner-voice ID at room distance is a soft prior at best and that vision + DOA must carry the addressee decision on Parcel.

findings.claim: A gaze+body-pose addressee estimator deployed in real time on the iCub needs a 0.8 s window and gives its first estimate in under 1 s, with only ~70% F1 on the 'robot is addressed' class.
findings.source_title: Real-time Addressee Estimation: Deployment of a Deep-Learning Model on the iCub Robot (Mazzola, Rea, Sciutti)
findings.numbers: 10-frame / 0.8 s sequences at 12.5 Hz; first estimate < 1 s; Vernissage test F1 overall 75.01% (robot 67.52 / left 78.61 / right 81.75); live on iCub with 6 participants in pairs: 75.84% (robot 71.73 / left 82.14 / right 76.33); companion paper arXiv 2308.10757 is CC-BY-4.0 with code/data on Zenodo
findings.relevance: Bounds what a camera-only addressee cue can deliver and its latency; it feeds the 0.5-2 Hz lane, not the 10 Hz act loop.

findings.claim: Large language models are worse than humans at addressee detection in online multi-party conversation and do not extract gaze from raw video, so the addressee decision should not be delegated to the LLM.
findings.source_title: Evaluating Large Language Models Abilities for Addressee, Turn-change, and Next Speaker Prediction in Meetings
findings.numbers: AMI 10 sessions / 4,051 utterances / 262 min / 16 speakers; human subset 347 utterances; chance 25%; addressee accuracy: humans 66.6%, Qwen3-14B 51.5%, Gemini 2.5 Pro 61.4%; next-speaker F1 humans 60.1%, Qwen3-14B 69.4%, Gemini 2.5 Pro 57.7%; human agreement alpha 0.67 (addressee) / 0.48 (next speaker); Gemini improved only when given explicit focus-of-attention labels
findings.relevance: Keeps the addressee gate in the local multimodal stack; the hosted LLM may re-rank but must not decide.

findings.claim: Speaker verification on a moving mobile robot at 1-3 m with its own actuator noise degrades from sub-1% VoxCeleb EER to 15-18% EER for a VoxCeleb-style ResNet-34, and even the close-talk reference channel gives 9.3%; the best challenge system reached 6.5%; noise-matched augmentation of the ENROLLMENT files helps.
findings.source_title: RoboVox: A Single/Multi-channel Far-field Speaker Recognition Benchmark for a Mobile Robot (LREC-COLING 2024) — with arXiv 2409.10240 and arXiv 2407.11365
findings.numbers: 78 speakers, ~11,000 dialogues, 8 channels (ch1-3 robot angles, ch4 in-body, ch5 close-talk); ResNet-34 baseline EER/DCT: ch1 15.79/0.92, ch2 15.63/0.87, ch3 15.74/0.88, ch4 18.22/0.91, ch5 9.29/0.73, multi-channel 15.06/0.86; DiPCo single-channel 5.84% vs RoboVox 18.22%; corpus CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. arXiv 2409.10240: 1/2/3 m, best no-aug ResNet EER 13.44 / DCF 0.84 -> 12.79 / 0.75 with -10..-4 dB robot noise added to enrollment; arXiv 2407.11365 (SP Cup 2024 2nd place): EER 6.46%, DCF 0.5245
findings.relevance: Sets the realistic owner-verification error budget on Parcel's body and the enrollment/augmentation recipe.

findings.claim: CAM++ matches or beats ECAPA-TDNN accuracy at half the parameters and ~2.5x faster single-thread CPU inference; together with the 3D-Speaker Apache-2.0 release it is the most deployable open speaker-embedding model found. No source measured any of these models on a Jetson.
findings.source_title: CAM++: A Fast and Efficient Network for Speaker Verification Using Context-Aware Masking (Interspeech 2023) — with 3D-Speaker GitHub https://github.com/modelscope/3D-Speaker
findings.numbers: CAM++ 7.18M params / 1.72 GFLOPs vs ECAPA-TDNN 14.66M / 3.96G vs ResNet34 6.70M / 6.84G; EER Vox1-O/E/H: CAM++ 0.73/0.89/1.76%, ECAPA 0.89/1.07/1.98%, ResNet34 0.97/1.03/1.88%; CN-Celeb 6.78% vs 7.45%; RTF single-thread CPU 0.013 vs 0.033 vs 0.032; 3D-Speaker table: CAM++ 7.2M 0.65%, ERes2NetV2 17.8M 0.61%, ECAPA 20.8M 0.86%, ERes2Net-base 6.61M 0.84%; Apache-2.0; ONNX runtime scripts
findings.relevance: Default per-utterance owner-verification backbone for the Orin; RTF 0.013 implies ~40 ms per 3 s utterance on one x86 thread, so GPU is unnecessary for this step.

findings.claim: Reference EER/size/license points for the other candidate speaker-verification backbones: ECAPA-TDNN (paper and SpeechBrain Apache-2.0 release), TitaNet (CC-BY-4.0), ReDimNet (1M-param B0), WavLM-Large (316M, best accuracy but far too large for per-frame use).
findings.source_title: ECAPA-TDNN (Interspeech 2020) — with SpeechBrain HF card https://huggingface.co/speechbrain/spkrec-ecapa-voxceleb , TitaNet https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2110.04410 and HF card https://huggingface.co/nvidia/speakerverification_en_titanet_large , ReDimNet https://arxiv.org/html/2407.18223v1 , WavLM https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2110.13900
findings.numbers: ECAPA C=512 6.2M / 1.01% Vox1-O (E 1.24, H 2.32); C=1024 14.7M / 0.87% (E 1.12, H 2.12); SpeechBrain spkrec-ecapa-voxceleb 0.80% EER, apache-2.0. TitaNet-S 6.4M / 1.15%, -M 13.4M / 0.81%, -L 25.3M / 0.68% (HF card: 23M, 0.66%, CC-BY-4.0). ReDimNet B0 1.0M / 0.43 GMACs / 1.16%, B1 2.2M / 0.85%, B2 4.7M / 0.57%, B6 15.0M / 0.40%. WavLM Base+ 94.7M, Large 316.6M; Large+ECAPA 0.617/0.662/1.318%, +LMFT+QAC 0.383/0.480/0.986%; ECAPA fbank baseline in that paper 1.080/1.200/2.127%
findings.relevance: Model-selection table for the owner-verification tier; sizes bound what can share the Orin with Model A.

findings.claim: A personal (target-speaker) voice activity detector conditioned on the enrolled speaker's embedding fits in ~1 MB / ~10 MFLOPs and is the right primitive for a continuous 'is the OWNER speaking' bit; the same idea (ECAPA target embedding + GRU) is what cut false barge-ins in an open full-duplex stack from 33-78% to 10%.
findings.source_title: Personal VAD 2.0: Optimizing Personal Voice Activity Detection for On-Device Speech Recognition (Google) — with FireRedChat https://arxiv.org/html/2509.06502
findings.numbers: Personal VAD 2.0: 1.0 MB quantized (vs 5.8 MB v1), 9.58 MFLOPs; Conformer standard VAD 0.7 MB / 8.77 MFLOPs; enrollment WER non-concat/concat 12.4/32.7 (v1 17.9/41.0); enrollment-less 7.0/10.1; train 2.6M utts (~1,600 h, 6,923 spk) + 35M pairs (~27,500 h). FireRedChat pVAD: ECAPA-TDNN target embedding + GRU, 2000 h Mandarin+English, 0-30 dB SNR mixtures; false barge-in rate FireRedChat 10.2% vs LiveKit 33.4% vs TEN 78.1%; T90 170 / 140 / 90 ms; EoT accuracy 94.9-96.0% vs 70.8-86.2% vs 94.4-95.8%; P50 e2e latency 2.341 / 3.598 / 3.375 s
findings.relevance: Defines Model B's owner barge-in mechanism and the current open-source performance ceiling (~10% false barge-ins at ~170 ms).

findings.claim: Speaker-embedding accuracy collapses on short windows: an ECAPA student distilled for short context recovers some of it, but 250 ms still gives far lower assignment accuracy than the whole utterance, so a reliable owner bit cannot be produced within one 100 ms act-loop tick.
findings.source_title: Towards Low-Latency Tracking of Multiple Speakers With Short-Context Speaker Embeddings (Iatariene, Guérin, Serizel)
findings.numbers: SpeechBrain ECAPA-TDNN 1024-ch teacher (VoxCeleb, 7,205 ids); student crops 250/500/750/1000/1500/2000/8000 ms; LibriJump 2-spk AssA: teacher 250 ms 46.8%, student 250 ms 54.8%, 750 ms 63.1%, whole 65.5%; 512-ch student within 1.7% of 1024-ch; students more overlap-robust at 800-3200 ms
findings.relevance: Fixes the timing contract: owner identity arrives 0.3-1 s after speech onset, in the language lane's cadence, not the 10 Hz loop's.

findings.claim: Acoustic-only addressee detection has a 20-year literature: acoustic-only EER moved from ~12.6% (2012) to ~5.5% (2021), acoustic UAR ~82% vs ~93% when semantics are added, with energy-based features the most important cue; corpora are small and demographically narrow.
findings.source_title: Acoustic-Based Automatic Addressee Detection for Technical Systems: A Review (Siegert, Weißkirchen, Wendemuth)
findings.numbers: Shriberg 2012 EER 12.63%; Tong 2021 EER 5.48%; Batliner 2009 74.2% acc (SVC: 4 h / 99 speakers); Akhtiamov 2017 UAR 82.2% acoustic (1,000 ComParE features), 92.9% acoustic+semantic; Tsai 2015 13.9% EER multimodal; VACC 17 h / 27 speakers; Amazon in-house up to 6M utterances (4M:2M); cues: duration, energy, F0, pauses, jitter, shimmer
findings.relevance: Prosody/energy features are cheap inputs for Parcel's Stage-A gate and Stage-C confirmation; also warns that published numbers rarely transfer across rooms/speakers.

design_implications: Model B owner gate is two-tier and fully local: a ~1 MB personal VAD conditioned on the owner's enrolled embedding runs every frame and is the only thing allowed to barge in on narration or open the hosted-voice stream; a per-utterance CAM++/ReDimNet embedding (Apache-2.0, ~40 ms on one CPU thread) confirms identity before a steering command is committed.

Plan for far-field owner-verification EER of ~10-18% on the Go2 body at 1-3 m (RoboVox), not the 0.4-1% of VoxCeleb; treat voice identity as a soft prior fused with XVF3800 direction-of-arrival and camera face/head-pose (Furhat: voice ID 18-27% correct vs face 80-95%), enroll the owner multi-room/multi-distance, and add recorded Go2 actuator/gait noise to the enrollment side.

Timing contract: the owner bit and the addressee bit land 0.3-1 s after speech onset (short-context embeddings are unreliable below ~750 ms; iCub gaze model needs 0.8 s), so voice steering enters through the 0.5-2 Hz language/plan lane; the 10 Hz act loop only gets a provisional 'speech from DOA theta' orienting cue.

Addressee gate follows the SAS/SDAR shape in front of the hosted voice: Stage A ~0.5 M-param audio-only classifier on the beamformed stream (expect F1 ~0.86, ~2% false triggers, ~8% with TV, <55 ms); Stage B an 8-10 s interaction state (robot just spoke / was just addressed / owner facing) which is worth ~38 F1 points and halves FAR at fixed FRR; Stage C the language lane's ASR text + confidence + prosody into the local LM (EER 7-8% class). Only Stage-C positives become plan edits or get forwarded to OpenAI Realtime, since neither OpenAI (no addressee option) nor Gemini 3.1 Flash Live (proactive_audio dropped) will filter side-talk server-side.

Camera fusion is the largest lever but range-limited (Google gates Look-and-Talk at 5 ft; SAS A+V F1 0.95): use head-pose toward the robot as a strong positive within ~1.5-2 m and neutral beyond, and have the 10 Hz loop turn the head toward the DOA on Stage-A/B positives so the camera can vote before Stage C.

Do not delegate addressee to the hosted or local LLM (humans 66.6% vs Qwen3-14B 51.5% / Gemini 2.5 Pro 61.4% on AMI; LLMs do not read gaze from raw video); the multimodal gate decides, the LLM at most re-ranks.

Barge-in during robot narration requires the TTS stream as a reference input to the personal VAD / DDSD nets (Amazon implicit AEC: -56% FRR during playback; Conversation Mode: -42% self-triggered false wakes); the open-source ceiling for speaker-gated barge-in is ~10% false barge-ins at T90 ~170 ms (FireRedChat pVAD) and should be the acceptance bar.

Data plan: every DDSD/addressee corpus with numbers is proprietary (Apple ~126 h, SAS 600 h, Amazon 6 M utterances) and SAS weights are unreleased, so Parcel must record its own robot-directed vs side-talk corpus through the XVF3800 on the real body (gait/actuator noise, 1-3 m, TV on, 1-4 people) with per-segment labels; usable open weights are SpeechBrain ECAPA (Apache-2.0), 3D-Speaker CAM++/ERes2NetV2 (Apache-2.0), TitaNet-L (CC-BY-4.0), WavLM-SV (UniSpeech license); RoboVox is CC BY-NC-SA (research only).

Open measurement gap to close in-house: no primary source times ECAPA/TitaNet/CAM++ on any Jetson; proxies (CAM++ RTF 0.013 on x86, 57-218 ms per 250 ms chunk on a Xeon in diart, SAS 38 ms on Cortex-A72) say the Orin has ample headroom, but the end-to-end owner+addressee decision must be benchmarked with the XVF3800 pipeline while the GPU is loaded by Model A.

results.claim: Wake-word-free, audio-only device-addressed speech detection runs on ARM Cortex-A72 (no GPU) in a 3-stage cascade (beamformer -> ~435K-param log-mel classifier -> ~85K-param causal Transformer over an 8 s rolling context); the 8 s interaction-state stage is the largest contributor (removing it drops F1 by 38 points). Weights are not released; corpus is proprietary.
results.evidence_quote: Stage 1: "A beamforming front-end localises the dominant speech source relative to the microphone array and suppresses off-axis interference (television audio, adjacent-room speech, HVAC)." Stage 2: "A lightweight 1D-convolutional classifier operating directly on 64-dimensional log-mel filterbank features (25 ms frames, 10 ms hop)" ... "The standard deployment variant (≈435 K parameters, ≈520 KB INT8-quantized)". Stage 3: "Total parameter count: ≈85 K of the system's 520 K parameters" ... "The context window is fixed at 8 seconds of interaction history". Ablation (Sec. 8.6, full model F1 0.95 / No Stage 1 0.81 / No Stage 2 0.74 / No Stage 3 0.57): "Stage 3 removal produces a 38-point F1 drop (bootstrap p<0.001), exceeding the combined effect of removing Stages 1 and 2." Hardware: "ARM Cortex-A72 at stock clock speeds on standard embedded Linux"; "GPU / NPU required: No"; "Hardware testing was conducted on Raspberry Pi 4 development boards and a Reachy Mini companion robot". Results: "F1 = 0.86 (precision = 0.89, recall = 0.83)" audio-only at tau=0.70, false trigger "2.1%" / "7.8%" with TV, single-mic "F1 = 0.84 (precision 0.88, recall 0.81)", A+V "F1 to 0.95 (precision = 0.97, recall = 0.93)", latency "median 38 ms, p95 51 ms" / "median 105 ms, p95 142 ms", "Total runtime footprint is under 20 MB." Data: "600-hour proprietary multi-speaker corpus", 60 h test, "1–4 speakers present", "28–85 dBA", "approximately 34% silent, 58% person-directed, and 8% device-directed". Release: "trained weights are not released but the functional interface is fully defined"; "The primary evaluation corpus is proprietary"; "no mandatory trigger phrase"; abs page: "All results are from internal evaluation on a proprietary dataset evaluated primarily in English".
results.correction: No correction needed. Two precision notes: (1) the 38-point drop is measured against the audio+video full model (0.95 -> 0.57±0.03), not the audio-only 0.86 figure; (2) the abs page lists no affiliation, so 'Attention Labs' in the source title is not verifiable from arXiv itself. Submitted 9 Apr 2026; internal evaluation only.

results.claim: The best published EER for device-directed speech detection without a wake word combines ASR 1-best text, acoustic embeddings and ASR decoder signals in an LLM; audio-only or text-only alone are ~11-13% EER, so a pre-ASR acoustic gate is necessary but not sufficient.
results.evidence_quote: Abstract: "Using multimodal information yields relative equal-error-rate improvements over text-only and audio-only models of up to 39% and 61%." Table 1: UM1 text-only (1-best) 12.70%; UM2 text-only +500k text 12.15%; UM3 DS-only 28.09%; UM4 audio-only Whisper 10.98% / CLAP 19.13%; MM6 "text+audio+DS" with 500k extra text: 7.95% (Whisper) / 7.45% (CLAP); "relative improvements of 27.6% and 61.1%" over audio-only; "relative EER improvements over the best performing text-only model (UM2) are 34.6% and 38.7%". Table 2: GPT-2 1.5B, LoRA "r=64, α=16": "EERs of 6.53% and 8.41%" (Whisper / CLAP). Data: "≈40k directed utterances (≈59 hours)", "≈40k non-directed utterances (≈67 hours)", "≈3 million randomized and anonymized utterances" text; eval "≈14k device-directed examples" / "≈23k non-directed examples" / "≈35 hours". Trigger status: "Approximately 21% of the device-directed examples in the training set start with a trigger phrase. The remaining device-directed utterances represent triggerless interactions." Prior-work comparison: none — the paper gives no comparative EER against prior literature and makes no state-of-the-art claim.
results.correction: All numbers in the claim are correct for this paper, but the superlative and the conclusion are not in the source. Corrected statement: In Apple's ICASSP 2024 study, fusing ASR 1-best text, Whisper/CLAP acoustic embeddings and ASR decoder signals in a GPT-2 classifier (MM6) reached 7.45–7.95% EER (6.53% with GPT-2 1.5B + Whisper, LoRA r=64), versus 12.15–12.70% text-only and 10.98% (Whisper) / 19.13% (CLAP) audio-only. The paper does not claim the 'best published' EER and contains no comparison to prior work; a later Apple follow-up (arXiv 2406.09617, Interspeech 2024, FLoRA) reports a further 22% relative EER reduction over text-only without absolute numbers, so 'best published' is unverified. The dataset is not purely wake-word-free (~21% of device-directed training utterances begin with a trigger phrase). 'A pre-ASR acoustic gate is necessary but not sufficient' is the author's inference, not a finding of the paper; note also that audio-only with CLAP is 19.13%, outside the '~11-13%' band, and the 34.6–38.7% text-only improvement is measured against UM2 (12.15%), not the 12.70% UM1 figure.

results.claim: Hosted voice APIs do not solve addressee for the robot: OpenAI Realtime offers only server_vad / semantic_vad plus interrupt/create flags with no documented option to ignore speech not directed at the model; Gemini Live's proactive_audio (model 'can proactively decide not to respond if the content is not relevant') is available only on the 2.5 Flash Live preview and is not supported on Gemini 3.1 Flash Live.
results.evidence_quote: Gemini capabilities page, Proactive audio section: "When this feature is enabled, Gemini can proactively decide not to respond if the content is not relevant. Note: This feature is not supported in Gemini 3.1 Flash Live. To use it, set the api version to v1beta and configure the proactivity field in the setup message and set proactive_audio to true" (code: client = genai.Client(http_options={"api_version": "v1beta"}); proactivity={'proactive_audio': True}). Model comparison table: Gemini 2.5 Flash Live Preview — "Proactive audio Supported. When enabled, the model can proactively decide not to respond if the input content is not relevant."; Gemini 3.1 Flash Live Preview — "Proactive audio Not supported". VAD parameters listed: start_of_speech_sensitivity, end_of_speech_sensitivity, prefix_padding_ms, silence_duration_ms; on interruption "the ongoing generation is canceled and discarded." No other mechanism to ignore non-addressed speech is documented. OpenAI Realtime VAD guide (https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/realtime-vad): server_vad fields "threshold: Activation threshold (0 to 1)", "prefix_padding_ms: Amount of audio (in milliseconds) to include before the VAD detected speech", "silence_duration_ms: Duration of silence (in milliseconds) to detect speech stop"; semantic_vad "eagerness" accepts "low" | "medium" | "high" | "auto" ("auto is the default value, and is equivalent to medium"); conversation-mode flags "create_response": true and "interrupt_response": true. The page contains no mention of addressee detection, speaker identification, or filtering non-directed speech.
results.correction: No correction needed. Minor wording: the table phrases it as 'if the input content is not relevant' while the section says 'if the content is not relevant'. The page's examples default to model gemini-3.1-flash-live-preview, so proactive audio requires explicitly selecting the 2.5 Flash Live Preview model plus v1beta. The 'no addressee gate' half of the claim rests on absence from documentation (both vendor pages), which is the appropriate standard for a documented-option claim but is not a positive statement by either vendor.

results.claim: On a social robot in real multi-party rooms, cloud voice-based speaker identification was nearly useless while face recognition and gaze-based turn-taking carried addressee detection; the system was ~92% correct on addressee with two parallel dyads and ~79% in a group, at ~1.35 s latency.
results.evidence_quote: "Thirty young adults participated in the study" (8 female, 22 male); "Participants were recruited in pairs to ensure familiarity and promote natural, fluent conversations... The experiment consisted of two open-ended scenarios. In both, participants sat facing the Furhat robot... A directional microphone array and a wide-angle camera were positioned in front of the participants." Pipeline: "The system combines voice and face recognition based on the voice direction of arrival and the face position in the video frame." Addressee: "To select the addressee, the conversation manager provides this conversation history and the list of recognised users from the face tracking module to the LLM, with the instructions to explicitly select an addressee and produce a response." Turn-taking: "The system takes the turn if the robot is looked at by the last speaker or after a prolonged silence." Table 2 (addressee): parallel 92.6% correct / 7.0% incorrect / 0.4% blank; group 79.3% correct / 13.6% incorrect / 7.2% blank ("blank denotes instances with no addressee detected or recognised"). Table 3: Azure voice recognition group 18.4% correct, 77.0% blank; parallel 26.8% correct, 72.8% blank; face recognition 80.0% (group) / 94.7% (parallel); "Audio-based speaker recognition emerged as a notably problematic component". Latency: "The average response delay was 1.35 s (SD = 0.55), occasionally reaching nearly 5 s... LLM generation time was the largest contributor to this delay (mean 0.76 s)." Stack: ReSpeaker DOA, Azure Cognitive Services speaker ID, face_recognition library + Furhat, GPT-3.5 streaming.
results.correction: All numbers hold, but two framing details are off. (1) Setting: this was a controlled lab study — 15 pairs of participants seated facing a Furhat with a mic array and camera in front of them — not 'real multi-party rooms' or in-the-wild (the relevance note's 'in-the-wild' is wrong). (2) Mechanism: addressee selection was made by the LLM (GPT-3.5) from the conversation history plus the list of users recognised by the face-tracking module, with speaker attribution from ReSpeaker DOA fused with face position; gaze ('robot is looked at by the last speaker') governed when the robot took the turn, not the addressee choice itself. 'Nearly useless' is the author's paraphrase of the paper's 'notably problematic' (18.4%/26.8% correct, 73-77% unrecognised). Corrected statement: In a lab study with 15 pairs, Azure cloud speaker ID correctly attributed only 18.4% (group) / 26.8% (parallel) of utterances, while face recognition (80.0% / 94.7%) fused with DOA fed an LLM-based addressee selector that was 92.6% correct in the parallel-dyad condition and 79.3% in the group condition, with gaze-based turn-taking and a mean response delay of 1.35 s (SD 0.55, up to ~5 s).

sweeps.topic: Unitree Go2 EDU SDK2/DDS command latency and rate limits (Move/Euler/LowCmd), unitree_sdk2py concurrency safety, and velocity-layer safety shields for learned navigation on quadrupeds

findings.claim: Since Go2 EDU firmware V1.1.6 (Motion Control Service V2.0, notice dated 2025-05-12) the sport-mode Move command is held by the robot for 1 second after the last message; Unitree instructs developers to filter velocities before sending and to send Move(0,0,0) or StopMove() when not commanding. Community reports on older firmware confirm the robot keeps moving until an explicit zero-velocity/StopMove is sent.
findings.source_title: Unitree Go2 Motion Control Service Interface V2.0 Update Notice (read via r.jina.ai mirror); corroborated by go2_ros2_sdk discussion #63
findings.numbers: firmware >= V1.1.6; notice 2025-05-12; 'the latest Move command will be maintained for 1 second'; vx [-2.5, 3.8] m/s, vy [-1.0, 1.0] m/s, vyaw [-4, 4] rad/s; example SetTimeout(10.0 s); discussion #63: robot 'will still move until kill the running thread', fixed by api 1008 with zeros then 1003
findings.relevance: Defines the only firm timing spec on the velocity interface; Parcel's gateway must own a sub-second watchdog and a slew/clamp filter in front of the 10 Hz act-token decoder.

findings.claim: In unitree_sdk2py, Move is the one sport call that is fire-and-forget (_CallNoReply, api 1008), while Euler (1007) and StopMove (1003) are blocking RPCs that wait on a response future with a 1.0 s default timeout; the C++ SDK has the same 1 s default. No lock protects _Call/_CallNoReply, and Channel.Write polls for a matched subscriber every 0.1 s up to the timeout before writing.
findings.source_title: unitree_sdk2_python sport_client.py, rpc/client_base.py, rpc/client_stub.py, core/channel.py; unitree_sdk2 client_base.hpp (BSD-3-Clause)
findings.numbers: SPORT_API_ID_MOVE=1008 via _CallNoReply; SPORT_API_ID_EULER=1007 and SPORT_API_ID_STOPMOVE=1003 via blocking _Call; default timeout 1.0 s (Python) / ROBOT_CLIENT_TIMEOUT=1000000 us 'default client timeout. 1s' (C++); request id = time.monotonic_ns(); Channel.Write polls publication-matched count in 0.1 s intervals; response receive queue depth 10; cyclonedds pinned to 0.10.2
findings.relevance: Tells the gateway which calls can sit on the 10 Hz act thread (Move) and which must go to a worker (Euler, StopMove, BodyHeight); single-writer serialisation is required because nothing in the client is locked.

findings.claim: Cyclone DDS's maintainer states the C API is thread-safe for reading/writing on the same or different entities; but cyclonedds-python's maintainer documents that listeners run synchronously with local-delivery writes under mutexes, so writing from an on_data_available callback that triggers another callback on the same entity deadlocks. unitree_sdk2py invokes subscriber handlers directly inside that listener thread whenever queueLen == 0.
findings.source_title: cyclonedds-python issue #7 (thijsmie) and cyclonedds issue #1913 (eboasson); unitree_sdk2py core/channel.py
findings.numbers: cyclonedds#1913: 'everything is thread-safe (... reading/writing on the same or different entities ...)' except topic filters; cyclonedds-python#7: 'listeners are called synchronously with a write on local delivery and protected by some mutexes this will deadlock'; unitree_sdk2py: queueLen>0 spawns daemon thread 'ch_reader', queueLen==0 'invokes the handler directly, bypassing the queue'; RequestFutureQueue is a dict under threading.Lock
findings.relevance: Concurrency rule for Parcel: state subscribers must use queueLen>0 or be polled from the gateway loop; never call SportClient from a DDS callback.

findings.claim: REASAN deploys a learned safety-shield network fully onboard a Unitree Go2 with a Livox Mid-360 and a Jetson AGX Orin 64 GB (Parcel's exact stack), running every module at 50 Hz via ONNX Runtime in ROS 2 nodes; the shield maps 180 LiDAR rays plus the nominal velocity command to a safe (vx, vy, wz) and achieved zero collisions across 40 real-world traversals.
findings.source_title: REASAN: Learning Reactive Safe Navigation for Legged Robots (arXiv 2512.09537)
findings.numbers: Go2 + Livox Mid-360 + Jetson AGX Orin (64 GB); 50 Hz all modules; 180 equidistant rays over 360 deg (2 deg spherical grid); estimator inference 1.3 +/- 0.1 ms (RTX 5090); sim SR 91.1 +/- 1.9 % (sparse), 79.1 +/- 4.4 % (dense), 95.2 +/- 2.9 % (maze), 68.2 +/- 2.3 % (dynamic maze); real 270 s / 180 s / 190 s / 180 s runs, 0 collisions in 40 traversals; multi-robot 93 s collision-free
findings.relevance: Existence proof that a velocity-layer shield fits Parcel's hardware at 5x the act-token rate; template for Model A's shield placement between act tokens and Move.

findings.claim: Point-cloud control barrier functions run onboard a Go2 (Jetson Orin NX) at 0.78 ms per CBF evaluation plus 0.37 ms local planning, filtering only the commanded linear and angular velocity fed to Unitree's proprietary controller, from a 16-channel LiDAR at 10 Hz with 1024 points per scan.
findings.source_title: Sailing Through Point Clouds: Safe Navigation Using Point Cloud Based Control Barrier Functions (arXiv 2403.18206)
findings.numbers: 16-channel 3D LiDAR at 10 Hz, 1024 points/scan; Go2 on Jetson Orin NX, B1 on Jetson AGX Orin; mean CBF time 0.78 ms (n_needle=100), local planner 0.37 ms; control input u = [v^T omega]^T in R^4; update layers 10 Hz / 2 Hz / once
findings.relevance: Compute budget for a CBF-QP shield inside Parcel's 100 ms act tick is negligible even on an Orin NX.

findings.claim: A safety-index QP over Go2 body-frame velocity commands at 30 Hz (command = measured + a*dt, dmin = 1 m) raised obstacle-course success from 60-80 % to 100 % after adapting the index to payload changes; adaptation costs 1.48 % of the full-synthesis compute.
findings.source_title: Safe Control of Quadruped in Varying Dynamics via Safety Index Adaptation (arXiv 2409.09882)
findings.numbers: Unitree Go2, high-level body-frame velocity commands; dt = 1/30 Hz; phi = dmin^2 - d^2 - 2 k d d-dot, dmin = 1 m; non-adapted 80 % (4/5), 60 % (3/5), 80 % (4/5); adapted 100 % (10/10, 6/6, 7/7); SIA = 1.48 % of synthesis time, finite-difference 96.5 % faster
findings.relevance: Gives a ready-made slew-filter + QP shape (velocity integrates acceleration at fixed dt) that matches Unitree's 'filter before sending' guidance.

findings.claim: Measured command-transmission latency through an LCM bridge on a Unitree robot (G1) is 18-30 ms with a 50 Hz policy and 500 Hz low-level loop; a Go2 RL deployment on a Jetson Orin NX holds 50 Hz control with 1000 Hz motor torque via Cyclone DDS + LCM within a 20 ms cycle. No paper measures Go2 sport-mode command-to-motion step response.
findings.source_title: From Language to Locomotion: Retargeting-free Humanoid Control via Motion Latent Guidance (arXiv 2510.14952), Sec. 6.4; and Learning Diverse Natural Behaviors ... (arXiv 2505.09979)
findings.numbers: 'Command transmission introduces a latency of 18-30ms'; policy 50 Hz; low-level 500 Hz; Go2/Orin NX: 50 Hz control, motors 1000 Hz, 20 ms cycle; depth 848x480 -> 87x58
findings.relevance: Best available bracket for the command delay Parcel's simulator should inject (20-50 ms) since a sport-mode step response is not published.

findings.claim: A single DDS hop on a Jetson Orin Nano carrying a Unitree 4D L1 LiDAR frame costs 0.685 ms mean with Fast DDS (1.593 ms with 10 readers), 0.839 ms with Zenoh; generic ROS 2 adds up to 50 % overhead over raw DDS for small messages and RELIABLE QoS up to 15 %.
findings.source_title: A Faster and More Reliable Middleware for Autonomous Driving Systems (arXiv 2510.11448); Kronauer et al., Latency Analysis of ROS2 Multi-Node Systems (arXiv 2101.02074)
findings.numbers: Orin Nano (8x Cortex-A78AE @ 2.2 GHz); L1 LiDAR 20 Hz, 2160 pts/frame: Fast DDS 0.685 ms (1->1), 1.593 ms (1->10); Zenoh 0.839 ms; camera 640x480@30: Fast DDS 3.40 ms, Zenoh 3.984 ms; SIM 0.226 ms (p99 0.382), 0.158 ms with SCHED_FIFO 99; Kronauer: ROS2 overhead up to 50 %, RELIABLE +15 %, RPi 4 overloaded >50 Hz at 13-17 nodes; CycloneDDS not in the 2025 test
findings.relevance: Transport on the Orin is sub-millisecond; the latency budget is dominated by the robot controller and the 1 s hold, not by DDS.

findings.claim: Remote bridges to Unitree dogs add tens to hundreds of ms: a WebRTC bridge on a Go2 Pro measured 33.9 ms mean network latency (1.75 s total gesture-to-motion reaction, 0.3 s debounce), and a Go1 Air app-protocol bridge measured 206.7 ms mean over Wi-Fi (std < 53 ms) vs 78.3 ms over Ethernet. WebRTC permits only one client connection at a time.
findings.source_title: Empowering the Unitree Go2 Pro for Elderly Care via WebRTC (Springer, abstract); Enabling Navigation and Mission-Based Control on a Low-Cost Unitree Go1 Air (Designs 2025, abstract via Semantic Scholar); legion1581/go2_webrtc_connect README
findings.numbers: 33.9 ms mean network latency; 1.75 s system reaction; 0.3 s debounce; 100 % on STOP/FOLLOW gestures; Go1 Air 206.7 ms Wi-Fi (std < 53 ms), 78.3 ms Ethernet; go2_webrtc_connect: RobotBusyError 'another WebRTC client is connected'; firmware 1.0.19-1.0.25, 1.1.1-1.1.14, 1.1.15+
findings.relevance: Rules out WebRTC/Wi-Fi as Parcel's control path and quantifies why the gateway must live on the Orin's eth0 DDS segment.

findings.claim: The community ROS 2 driver go2_ros2_sdk publishes sport requests on rt/api/sport/request with no velocity clamping or dead-zone and no visible cmd_vel watchdog, its driver loop sleeps 0.1 s (~10 Hz), and over WebRTC it receives LiDAR at 7 Hz and joint states at only 1 Hz (firmware-limited).
findings.source_title: go2_ros2_sdk README and source (command_generator.py, go2_driver_node.py), BSD-2-Clause
findings.numbers: SPORT_MODE_TOPIC = 'rt/api/sport/request'; parameters {'x','y','z'}; api 1008 move, 1003 obstacle-avoid move; asyncio.sleep(0.1); LiDAR 7 Hz (was ~2 Hz); joint states 1 Hz with firmware v1.1.7; 1k stars, 213 forks; firmware 1.1.15+ uses per-device AES-128 WebRTC keys
findings.relevance: Shows that the popular reference driver provides none of the filtering, clamping, or watchdog Unitree recommends; Parcel's gateway must implement them itself.

findings.claim: Switching a Go2 from sport mode to low-level joint control is not bumpless: ReleaseMode drops all joint torques momentarily, SelectMode('normal') within ~10 s of ReleaseMode returns error 7002, and publishing LowCmd while sport mode is active produces violent shaking; the official low-level example runs a 500 Hz (2 ms) CRC32-checked LowCmd loop after polling ReleaseMode at 5 s intervals.
findings.source_title: MYBOTSHOP forum '[Unitree Go2] mode switch'; ric.engineering 'How to disable sport mode on the Go2'; umi-on-legs codebase_setup.md; unitree_sdk2 example go2_stand_example.cpp
findings.numbers: error 7002 within ~10 s of ReleaseMode(); torque dropout on ReleaseMode; 2000 us recurrent thread (500 Hz); CRC32 polynomial 0x04c11db7; ReleaseMode retry every 5 s; msc.SetTimeout(10.0 s); ric.engineering SetTimeout(5.0), 1 s sleeps
findings.relevance: Keeps Parcel's Model A on the sport velocity API for the current milestone; joint-space control is a separate real-time engineering problem.

findings.claim: The Go2's DDS domain 0 is unauthenticated: any host on the robot network can publish request topics, which led to CVE-2026-27509 (unauthenticated RCE via rt/api/programming_actuator/request, api_id 1002) on EDU firmware V1.1.7-V1.1.11; 67 topics were discoverable on V1.1.7, reduced to 4 on V1.1.11.
findings.source_title: From DDS Packets to Robot Shells: Two RCEs in Unitree Robots (CVE-2026-27509 & CVE-2026-27510)
findings.numbers: DDS domain 0; no authentication by default; 67 active topics on V1.1.7, 4 on V1.1.11; CVE-2026-27509 (V1.1.7-V1.1.11 EDU) and CVE-2026-27510; eth0 192.168.123.161, wlan0 192.168.1.7; api_id 1002 on rt/api/programming_actuator/request
findings.relevance: Network isolation of the sport request topic is a safety property: the gateway must bind DDS to eth0 only and the Starlink/Wi-Fi side (hosted voice, Model B) must never bridge into domain 0.

findings.claim: Unitree's built-in obstacle avoidance is forward-only and its LiDAR-based stop envelope belongs to the navigation service, not the sport API: nav speed is capped at 0.2-1.0 m/s on Go2, stop mode (mode 1) halts on obstacles, bypass mode needs a 0.8 m corridor and obstacles <= 0.5 m wide and >= 20 cm tall; the manual asks operators to keep >= 2 m from people and obstacles and provides a damping-mode soft e-stop.
findings.source_title: Unitree SLAM and Navigation Services Interface (via r.jina.ai); Go2 User Manual V1.0 (PDF); ObstaclesAvoidClient source
findings.numbers: Go2 nav 0.2-1.0 m/s, Go2-W 0.2-1.5 m/s; mode 1 = stop, 0 = bypass; corridor >= 0.8 m, obstacle <= 0.5 m wide, >= 20 cm high; target <= 10 m; SLAM <= 30 min (thermal); L1 min range 0.05 m, 360x90 deg, 'only support forward obstacle avoidance'; keep >= 2 m from obstacles/crowds; L2+B = damping mode soft e-stop; ObstaclesAvoidClient api ids 1001 SwitchSet, 1002 SwitchGet, 1003 Move (no-reply), 1004 UseRemoteCommandFromApi
findings.relevance: Parcel cannot rely on the vendor for a person-aware stop envelope while driving through the sport API; the shield in the gateway has to provide it from the Mid-360.

findings.claim: Other hardware-validated shields on Go1/Go2 all sit at the velocity/twist layer at 10-50 Hz: UEREBot's CBF shield on Go2 + Mid-360 + Orin NX reached 75 % goal / 64 % task success over 200 real trials against obstacles trained at 0.5-4.0 m/s; ABS switches agile/recovery policies at a reach-avoid value threshold of -0.05 (3.1 m/s peak on Go1/Orin NX); the OCR 'One Filter' overrides twist from a 100-ray LiDAR scan with 10/10 success and 0 collisions on normal floors; Shield-Loco filters contact targets at 3 Hz on an offboard RTX 3090 (~200-400 ms per cycle).
findings.source_title: UEREBot (arXiv 2602.07363); ABS (arXiv 2401.17583); One Filter to Deploy Them All (arXiv 2412.09989); Shield-Loco (arXiv 2606.07193); SEA-Nav (arXiv 2603.09460)
findings.numbers: UEREBot: body-frame [vx vy w]; path 10-20 Hz, predictions 50 Hz; obstacle speeds U(0.5, 4.0) m/s; 200 trials: 75 % goal, 70 % avoidance, 64 % task. ABS: Vthreshold = -0.05; 3.1 m/s peak; sim SR 79.1 +/- 4.4 %, collision 5.7 +/- 2.9 %. One Filter: Go1 + RPLiDAR A2, 100 rays [0.2, 10] m; hardware 10 trials/row, best 10/0/0, slippery 8/1/1. Shield-Loco: 3 Hz, K=512, N=3, H=5; H=6 ~200 ms, H=8 ~400 ms; violations ~300+ -> ~30. SEA-Nav: 41 rays [-2pi/3, 2pi/3], 0.1-3.0 m; 10 Hz extero / 50 Hz proprio; sim hard SR 90.00 +/- 1.63 %, collision 5.00 %
findings.relevance: Confirms the design pattern (filter [v, w], keep the vendor gait controller) and gives the realistic success-rate ceiling (64-75 %) against fast dynamic obstacles even with a shield.

design_implications: Gateway watchdog under the 1 s hold: Model A's 10 Hz act tokens map 1:1 to Move(vx,vy,vyaw); a stalled Model A or Python thread keeps the dog moving up to 1 s, so the gateway must own a 200-300 ms watchdog that emits Move(0,0,0) then StopMove(), tested in the sim loop with a frozen Model A.

Filter and clamp in the act-token decoder, as Unitree instructs and the reference ROS driver omits: hard limits vx [-2.5, 3.8], vy [-1, 1], vyaw [-4, 4]; companion envelope near the vendor nav range (0.2-1.0 m/s); slew-limit via command = measured + a*dt (the 30 Hz safety-index form).

Velocity-layer shield inside the 10 Hz tick: Mid-360 -> 180-ray polar reduction -> CBF-QP or learned shield (REASAN-style) -> clamped Move; sub-millisecond cost on Orin-class hardware; the shield may only reduce speed, act tokens stay nominal; it also provides the person-aware stop envelope the vendor's forward-only avoidance does not.

Single writer, single thread: no lock guards _CallNoReply/_Call and Channel.Write can block to the timeout; serialise all sport calls through one gateway thread; Model B steering enters via Model A's plan/act lane (submit/suspend/resume/amend), never a second SportClient; blocking calls (StopMove, Euler, BodyHeight, mode switches) run on a separate worker with explicit SetTimeout, never on the 10 Hz thread.

Never write from a DDS callback: create LowState/SportModeState/LiDAR subscribers with queueLen > 0 or poll them from the gateway loop; Move inside a queueLen=0 handler is the cyclonedds-python deadlock pattern and a blocking Euler there stalls DDS delivery for the process.

Expression-lane budget: Euler (roll/pitch +/-0.75 rad, yaw +/-0.6 rad) and BodyHeight ([-0.18, 0.03] m) are 1 s-timeout RPCs; at most one per hold window, from the worker thread, suppressed by the shield when speed is non-zero; use ContinuousGait for idle liveness at zero velocity.

Simulator fidelity: model the 1 s command hold, a randomised 20-100 ms command-to-controller delay (18-30 ms measured through a Unitree bridge plus sub-ms DDS), 50 Hz state feedback on lf/ topics (never the 1 Hz WebRTC joint states), and the shield's speed reduction; train Model A under that delay alongside the 0-10 s plan-lane delay already borrowed from TIC-VLA.

Mode discipline for this milestone: stay on the sport (mcf) velocity API; sport->low-level handoff costs a torque dropout, a ~10 s cooldown (error 7002), and a 500 Hz CRC-checked real-time loop; joint-space Model A is a later, separately gated milestone.

Network hygiene as safety: bind ChannelFactoryInitialize(0, 'eth0') to the robot's 192.168.123.x segment only; DDS domain 0 is unauthenticated (CVE-2026-27509) so the Starlink/Wi-Fi side carrying hosted voice and Model B must never bridge into it; WebRTC is single-client and unsuitable as a control path.

Hardware evidence to collect when a Go2 is available (absent from the public record): Move step response at 10 Hz, _CallNoReply jitter from Python on the AGX Orin under Model A load, actual lf/sportmodestate rate, hold behaviour with ObstaclesAvoidClient.UseRemoteCommandFromApi(True), and whether error 4201 fires on Euler during motion.

results.claim: Since Go2 EDU firmware V1.1.6 (Motion Control Service V2.0, notice dated 2025-05-12) the sport-mode Move command is held by the robot for 1 second after the last message; Unitree instructs developers to filter velocities before sending and to send Move(0,0,0) or StopMove() when not commanding. Community reports on older firmware confirm the robot keeps moving until an explicit zero-velocity/StopMove is sent.
results.evidence_quote: Heading: 'Motion Control Service Interface V2.0 Update Notice' / 'Release Date: May 12, 2025' / 'Go2 officially releases V1.1.6' / 'Applicability: This document's interfaces apply to Go2 Edu models with software version >= V1.1.6.' / Move Notes: 'The Move interface has two characteristics: (1) The motion control part does not filter the Move command; (2) The latest Move command will be maintained for 1 second. Recommendation: When using this interface, apply filtering before sending; when not using Move, send Move(0,0,0) or StopMove().' / Parameters: 'vx: Range [-2.5~3.8] (m/s); vy: Range [-1.0~1.0] (m/s); vyaw: Range [-4~4] (rad/s).' / 'sport_client.SetTimeout(10.0f); // Set timeout'. Discussion #63 (Lin-jun-xiang, Jul 18 2024): 'After the while loop completing, the go2 will still move until kill the running thread.' with fix 'conn.data_channel.send(gen_command(1008, x=0., y=0, z=0)); conn.data_channel.send(gen_command(1003)) # StopMove'.
results.correction: All numbers verified (the direct support.unitree.com URL renders only a JS shell; the r.jina.ai mirror carries the full text). Minor caveats to carry: (a) the vendor page also states the motion controller 'does not filter the Move command', which strengthens the filter-before-send requirement; (b) discussion #63 is dated July 2024, ten months before the V1.1.6 notice, so 'older firmware' is a date inference — no participant states a firmware version — and it uses the WebRTC data channel (go2_webrtc, api ids 1008/1003) rather than unitree_sdk2py; it is a single-user report.

results.claim: In unitree_sdk2py, Move is the one sport call that is fire-and-forget (_CallNoReply, api 1008), while Euler (1007) and StopMove (1003) are blocking RPCs that wait on a response future with a 1.0 s default timeout; the C++ SDK has the same 1 s default. No lock protects _Call/_CallNoReply, and Channel.Write polls for a matched subscriber every 0.1 s up to the timeout before writing.
results.evidence_quote: sport_client.py: 'def Move(self, vx: float, vy: float, vyaw: float): ... code = self._CallNoReply(SPORT_API_ID_MOVE, parameter)' (the only _CallNoReply call in the file); 'def Euler(...): code, data = self._Call(SPORT_API_ID_EULER, parameter)'; 'def StopMove(self): code, data = self._Call(SPORT_API_ID_STOPMOVE, parameter)'. sport_api.py: 'SPORT_API_ID_MOVE = 1008', 'SPORT_API_ID_EULER = 1007', 'SPORT_API_ID_STOPMOVE = 1003'. client_base.py: 'self.__timeout = 1.0' ... 'future = self.__stub.SendRequest(request, self.__timeout)' ... 'result = future.GetResult(self.__timeout)' ... 'identity = RequestIdentity(time.monotonic_ns(), apiId)'. client_base.hpp: '@default client timeout. 1s' / 'const int64_t ROBOT_CLIENT_TIMEOUT = 1000000;'. channel.py Write: 'while waitsec > 0.0 and self.__publication_matched_count == 0: time.sleep(0.1); waitsec = waitsec - 0.1'. client_stub.py: 'CreateRecvChannel(..., Response, self.__ResponseHandler,10)'. setup.py: '"cyclonedds==0.10.2"'. No threading.Lock in client.py, client_base.py or client_stub.py; the only Lock is 'self.__lock = Lock()' inside RequestFutureQueue.
results.correction: Every number checks out. Two precision notes: (1) `_Call`/`_CallNoReply` live in rpc/client.py and delegate to `_CallBase`/`_CallNoReplyBase` in rpc/client_base.py; (2) the 1.0 s timeout is applied twice on a blocking call — first as Channel.Write's matched-subscriber wait (up to 1 s), then as future.GetResult (up to 1 s) — so the worst-case block for Euler/StopMove is ~2 s, not 1 s. Also, sport_client.py has no BodyHeight method (mentioned only in the relevance note).

results.claim: Cyclone DDS's maintainer states the C API is thread-safe for reading/writing on the same or different entities; but cyclonedds-python's maintainer documents that listeners run synchronously with local-delivery writes under mutexes, so writing from an on_data_available callback that triggers another callback on the same entity deadlocks. unitree_sdk2py invokes subscriber handlers directly inside that listener thread whenever queueLen == 0.
results.evidence_quote: cyclonedds-python #7 'Thread deadlock when attempting to transmit data from Listener callback' (opened by pbleyer 2021-05-26), thijsmie 2021-05-26: 'After some review and a quick chat with @eboasson I think the issue here is that you generate a `on_data_available` callback within another `on_data_available` callback. Since listeners are called synchronously with a write on local delivery and protected by some mutexes this will deadlock.' cyclonedds #1913 'Question: what is thread-safe?' (opened by Aposhian 2023-12-30), eboasson 2024-01-12: 'In principle everything is thread-safe (that includes creating/deleting domains and entities, reading/writing on the same or different entities, waiting for data or events, attaching/detaching entries from waitsets, messing around with changeable QoS settings and listeners, ...). The topic filters are a really rare deviation from this general rule.' unitree_sdk2py core/channel.py: 'if queueLen > 0: ... self.__threadReader = Thread(target=self.__ChannelReaderThreadFunc, name="ch_reader", daemon=True)'; inside __OnDataAvailable: 'if self.__queueEnable: self.__queue.Put(sample) else: self.__handler(sample)'. request_future.py: 'self.__data = {}' / 'self.__lock = Lock()'.
results.correction: Substance fully supported (both maintainer quotes are verbatim, retrieved via the GitHub comments API since the issue HTML fetch omits comments). One wording fix: the phrase 'invokes the handler directly, bypassing the queue' in the numbers field is a paraphrase, not a source comment — the code is simply the else-branch `self.__handler(sample)` inside `__OnDataAvailable`. Also thijsmie describes 'a callback within another callback' on local delivery; he does not literally say 'same entity'.

results.claim: REASAN deploys a learned safety-shield network fully onboard a Unitree Go2 with a Livox Mid-360 and a Jetson AGX Orin 64 GB (Parcel's exact stack), running every module at 50 Hz via ONNX Runtime in ROS 2 nodes; the shield maps 180 LiDAR rays plus the nominal velocity command to a safe (vx, vy, wz) and achieved zero collisions across 40 real-world traversals.
results.evidence_quote: 'We deploy REASAN fully onboard a Unitree Go2 robot equipped with a Livox Mid-360 LiDAR and a Jetson AGX Orin (64 GB) ... The trained neural networks are exported from PyTorch to ONNX format, using ONNX Runtime for fast onboard inference, with each module wrapped as a ROS2 node.' / 'all modules maintain stable real-time performance at 50 Hz over 60 s' / 'the safety-shield policy, which transforms the high-level navigation velocity command into a safe one for locomotion given the 180-ray exteroception' / velocity commands '(v_x, v_y, omega_z), representing two-dimensional linear and angular velocity in the base frame' / 'spherical grid with an angular resolution of 2° in both azimuth and elevation' / Table III REASAN '1.3±0.1' ms on 'a single GeForce RTX 5090 GPU (batch size 1)' / sim SR 91.1±1.9, 79.1±4.4, 95.2±2.9, 68.2±2.3 / 'We conduct experiments in four different scenarios within a 40 m² test ground ... the robot is required to traverse between two locations 10 times autonomously while handling various conditions: Static ...; Dynamic ...; and DeadEnd .... Additionally, we introduce Herding, where only the safety-shield policy is activated with zero commanded velocity, and the robot is guided purely through collision-avoidance reactions as a person herds it between two ends for 5 rounds.' / 'the robot exhibits no collisions with any obstacle' / Table IV durations 'Static Dynamic DeadEnd Herding ... 270 180 190 180' / 'the experiment runs for 93 s without any collision'.
results.correction: Hardware, onboard deployment, ONNX Runtime + ROS 2, 50 Hz, 180 rays, 2° grid, 1.3 ms, sim success rates, run durations, zero collisions and the 93 s multi-robot run are all verified. The figure '40 real-world traversals' is not in the paper: it states 10 autonomous traversals between two locations (across the Static, Dynamic and DeadEnd scenarios) plus a 5-round shield-only Herding test; the '40' is the 40 m² area of the test ground. Corrected statement: 'zero collisions across the 10-traversal navigation tests (Static/Dynamic/DeadEnd) and a 5-round shield-only Herding test, totalling ~820 s of collision-free onboard operation.' Paper is dated 10 Dec 2025 (arXiv 2512.09537, Yuan, Cao, Cao, Li).

findings.claim: Qwen-RobotNav-4B (Qwen3-VL + 4-layer MLP head, 8 waypoints) runs on a Unitree Go2 with an on-board Jetson Thor at 204 ms per step (4.9 Hz) using FP8 quantization and TensorRT, versus 196 ms (5.1 Hz) via a remote server, and its weights are not released.
findings.source_title: Qwen-RobotNav Technical Report: A Scalable Navigation Model Designed for an Agentic Navigation System
findings.numbers: Sizes 2B/4B/8B; on-device Thor FP8 + TensorRT 204 ms (4.9 Hz); remote 196 ms (5.1 Hz); 'on-device inference ... provided much more consistent latency'; output K=8 waypoints (x,y,theta); Figure 11: Qwen-RobotNav-4B on Unitree Go2; frames/visual-token budget used on robot not stated; report CC BY 4.0; repo: 'There is currently no plan to release the model weights'. Thor/Orin VLM ratio ~1.65x and Orin lacks FP8, so a derived Orin INT4 port is ~2-3 Hz (unmeasured).
findings.relevance: The closest thing to a ~5 Hz navigation VLM on a robot; it needed Thor + FP8, which bounds what a 4B navigator can do on Parcel's Orin.

findings.claim: On Jetson AGX Orin 64 GB the vision encoder alone costs 98-160 ms per frame in FP16 (PaliGemma2 SigLIP 98.5 ms, Qwen3-VL-2B SigLIP-2 160.6 ms), eager-transformers decode is 90-138 ms per token for 0.5-3B VLMs, BitsAndBytes INT4 on the LLM raises TPOT by 32-56 % (VRAM -22 to -48 %), and INT8 on SigLIP encoders makes them 2.4-4.7x slower, because Orin's Ampere has no INT4 tensor path.
findings.source_title: Rethinking Small VLM Quantization: From Component-Wise Analysis to Hardware-Aware Edge Deployment (ETRI, ICML 2026 workshop)

design_implications: Model A's 10 Hz act-token loop cannot contain a language model on the AGX Orin: the fastest measured VLM step is 150 ms (SmolVLM-256M Q4, 6.6 Hz) and RhinoVLA's roofline says a 3B VLM+action-expert already saturates the Orin at 5 Hz; the only 10 Hz-class numbers (pi0 27.9 ms, GR00T 26.7 ms) are amortised over action chunks. Keep the 10 Hz lane a small non-LM policy (or a chunked action head) that reads a goal/latent written asynchronously by the VLM lane, exactly as TIC-VLA does (10 Hz policy + 0.5 Hz VLM, 0.75 SR on a Go2's Orin NX).

Size Model A's language/plan lane by its input-memory and output budget, not by parameter count alone: on AGX Orin a <=2B VLM is ~2 Hz for 1-2 frames and <=16 output tokens, ~1 Hz with an 8-frame x 196-token memory (prefill ~0.45 s + decode); a 3-4B model is ~0.5 Hz with the 8-frame memory; a 7-8B model is 1-2.7 Hz only for a single image and <=8 tokens (OpenVLA INT4 375 ms) and 0.2-0.3 Hz with an 8-frame plan (2.27 s prefill FP16 + 32 tokens at 10-40 tok/s). InternVL3-1B/2B and Qwen3-VL-2B (TensorRT Edge-LLM INT4-AWQ) are the on-Orin candidates; 7-8B belongs to the hosted side.

Cache vision tokens per frame and never re-encode the memory: SigLIP-class encoders cost 98-160 ms per frame FP16 on AGX Orin (8 fresh frames = 0.8-1.3 s before any LLM work) and an unoptimised llama.cpp mmproj took 4.1 s for one image. Encode each frame once (at the plan-lane rate or on scene change), keep 196 tokens/frame in a ring buffer, prefill only the newest frame + text; keep the vision tower FP16 (INT8 on SigLIP is 2.4-4.7x slower on Orin).

Make the plan lane's output a fixed, short structured object (waypoints / subgoal id / act-token prior, <=16-32 tokens) or a latent/KV handoff, never on-device chain-of-thought: TIC-VLA's 1B took 4.8 s per step on an Orin NX because it writes reasoning text, while REIS's 3B affordance check with zero output tokens is 406 ms on the same part and EdgeReasoning shows decode dominating prefill 192-569x. This also makes the lane period deterministic, which the 10 Hz loop and the sim-to-real latency injection need.

Treat the inference runtime as a first-class deliverable and report every latency with runtime, precision and nvpmodel: eager transformers gives 136 ms/token for Qwen3-VL-2B on AGX Orin, vLLM AWQ gives 32 ms/token for a 3B on an Orin NX, MLC INT4 gives 40-47 tok/s for 7-8B; BitsAndBytes INT4 makes Orin slower (+56 % TPOT) because Ampere has no INT4 tensor path; llama.cpp prompt-processing on Orin is 48 tok/s for 8B (unusable for 1.5k-token prefills); a misconfigured vLLM ran 7x below NVIDIA's reproduction (30 vs 225 tok/s). Target TensorRT Edge-LLM INT4-AWQ (JetPack 7.2) or vLLM w4a16, at MAXN + jetson_clocks, and re-measure at 30 W.

Keep the on-Orin part of Model B small and time-multiplex it with Model A: a 7-8B text model decodes at ~10 tok/s FP16 / ~40 tok/s INT4 on an idle Orin (a 30-token narration = 0.75-3 s) and would halve Model A's lane while running; no published co-scheduling measurement exists, so Parcel should produce one. Local Model B should be a <=3B INT4 model (75-110 tok/s SLM class) or a steering classifier that emits receipts for the hosted Realtime voice; local narration is only the Starlink-dropout fallback. Pipeline Model A prefill (compute-bound) against Model B decode (memory-bound) rather than running two decodes at once.

Evaluate in sim with the Orin-measured lane latency injected and train Model A under randomised 0.5-5 s plan-lane delays: TIC-VLA lost 10 SR points (0.85 -> 0.75) moving from a laptop GPU to an Orin NX purely from latency. Use the W3 numbers (~1 s for <=2B, ~2 s for 3-4B, 3-5 s for 7-8B) as the injected delays.

Treat Jetson Thor as the scale-up path, not the baseline: Thor is 1.6x AGX Orin on VLM throughput and 2.5-2.7x on VLAs, adds FP8/NVFP4, and is where the only ~5 Hz robot navigator (Qwen-RobotNav-4B, 204 ms) and the 54 ms pi0.5 live; a 4B navigator at >=2 Hz with real memory on the Orin is a derived estimate (~2-3 Hz), unmeasured. Memory (64 GB) is not the constraint on the Orin; the 204.8 GB/s bus and kernel utilisation are.

Licensing gates the candidates: TIC-VLA code/weights are under a non-commercial UCLA Academic Software License (study only), Qwen-RobotNav weights are unreleased, Moondream is permissive for commercial use; the measurement papers (EdgeReasoning, small-VLM quantization, Qwen-RobotNav report) are CC BY 4.0. Base a shippable Model A on InternVL3 / Qwen3-VL / Moondream-class weights with a licence Parcel has read, not on TIC-VLA's checkpoint.

results.claim: On Jetson AGX Orin 64 GB the vision encoder alone costs 98-160 ms per frame in FP16 (PaliGemma2 SigLIP 98.5 ms, Qwen3-VL-2B SigLIP-2 160.6 ms), eager-transformers decode is 90-138 ms per token for 0.5-3B VLMs, BitsAndBytes INT4 on the LLM raises TPOT by 32-56 % (VRAM -22 to -48 %), and INT8 on SigLIP encoders makes them 2.4-4.7x slower, because Orin's Ampere has no INT4 tensor path.
results.evidence_quote: Table 3: "Jetson Orin AGX ... 64GB LPDDR5 ... 204.8 GB/s ... Jetpack 6.2.1". Table 6 (FP16 vision encoding, ms, NX/AGX): PaliGemma2 SigLIP-So400m "311.9 ... 98.5", Qwen3-VL SigLIP-2 "394.6 ... 160.6", LLaVA-OV "719.8 ... 381.2", DS-VL2 "1,423.3 ... 903.5", Kosmos-2.5 "11,029.2 ... 2,903.6"; INT8 ratios AGX ×4.66 / ×3.11 / ×2.43 / ×2.51 / ×1.20. Table 7 AGX: "Qwen3-VL 4.06 2.13 -47.5% 136.2 212.4 +55.9%; PaliGemma2 5.85 3.18 -45.6% 137.9 182.1 +32.0%; LLaVA-OV 2.25 1.76 -21.8% 90.5 141.4 +56.3%". "LLM INT4 (cfg1) lowers the VRAM usage by 21.8–47.5% but raises the TPOT by 10.4–56.3% across all platforms (Table 7). These empirical results demonstrate that within the Jetson Orin Ampere architecture, the dequantization overhead introduced by BitsAndBytes outweighs the native computation speedup provided by INT4 ... LLM INT4 implemented via BitsAndBytes should be viewed purely as a VRAM-saving approach, rather than as a technique for reducing latency." Sec 3.1: "If native INT4 operation support is limited in the Ampere architecture of Jetson Orin, the TPOT may increase". Appendix F: "The AWQ baseline nearly preserves the MME accuracy of the FP16/BF16 baseline and, unlike BitsAndBytes INT4, does not reproduce the TPOT penalty, indicating that the TPOT increase under BitsAndBytes LLM INT4 is tied to the BitsAndBytes execution path in our runtime, rather than being an inherent property of 4-bit LLM quantization." (Table 18: FP16 111.1 ms, BnB INT4 173.1 ms, AWQ W4A16 107.5 ms). Appendix E: the INT8 anomaly "arises from the interaction between SigLIP-style encoders, the BitsAndBytes INT8 execution path, and the Jetson Orin Ampere architecture, rather than from any inherent inefficiency of SigLIP or of INT8 vision quantization in general." results.correction: All numbers are correct for AGX Orin (vision FP16 98.5 / 160.6 ms; TPOT 90.5-137.9 ms; INT4 TPOT +32.0 to +56.3 %, VRAM -21.8 to -47.5 %; INT8 SigLIP ×2.43-4.66). Two fixes: (1) drop 'because Orin's Ampere has no INT4 tensor path' — the paper only hedges ('If native INT4 operation support is limited...') and explicitly attributes the slowdown to BitsAndBytes dequantization overhead; its Appendix F shows AWQ W4A16 on the same AGX/NX incurs no TPOT penalty (107.5 ms vs 111.1 ms FP16), and the INT8 SigLIP anomaly is attributed to the BitsAndBytes INT8 kernel path on Ampere, not to missing tensor-core support. Corrected wording: 'BitsAndBytes INT4/INT8 kernels on Orin's Ampere add dequantization overhead that outweighs any speedup; AWQ W4A16 does not show the penalty, so use AWQ/TensorRT kernels.' (2) The paper never says 'eager'; state instead 'HF-style generate() via VLMEvalKit wrappers, greedy decoding, no compiled runtime'. Also note the 98-160 ms vision range covers only the two named SigLIP models; the paper's AGX vision-encoder range across all five models is 98.5-2903.6 ms (LLaVA-OV 381.2, DeepSeek-VL2 903.5).
